From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

International award for parks and green spaces

For the unrelated roadside assistance company, see [Green Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag "Green Flag").

The **Green Flag Award** is an international accreditation given to publicly accessible parks and open spaces, managed under licence from the [Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Levelling_Up,_Housing_and_Communities "Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities"), a UK Government department, by [Keep Britain Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Britain_Tidy "Keep Britain Tidy"), which also administers the scheme in England.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Green Flag Award was introduced in 1996, and first awarded in 1997, by the [Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Housing,_Communities_and_Local_Government "Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government") (MHCLG) with the intention of establishing agreed standards of good management, to help to justify and evaluate funding and to raise park attendance. The scheme was managed by [Civic Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Trust_(England) "Civic Trust (England)"), on MHCLG's behalf, until they lost the contract and the charity went bust in 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-1)

The scheme has been managed by Keep Britain Tidy since 2012,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-2) with sister organisations [Keep Scotland Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Scotland_Beautiful "Keep Scotland Beautiful"), [Keep Wales Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Wales_Tidy "Keep Wales Tidy") and [TIDY Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TIDY_Northern_Ireland "TIDY Northern Ireland") delivering the scheme across the UK, and various other bodies delivering worldwide.

## Purpose and description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Purpose and description")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg/250px-Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg)[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Boscombe_Chine_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg/250px-Boscombe_Chine_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boscombe_Chine_Gardens,_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg)
[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg/250px-Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg)
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Bournemouth_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg/250px-Bournemouth_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bournemouth_Gardens,_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg)
Green Flags on Display in [Manor Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manor_Park,_London "Manor Park, London"), London; [Boscombe Chine Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe "Boscombe"), Dorset; [Baysgarth Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baysgarth_Park "Baysgarth Park"), Lincolnshire; and [Bournemouth Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth_Gardens,_England "Bournemouth Gardens, England"), Dorset.

The scheme's aim is to promote standards of good management and best-practice amongst the green space sector. It is described by its issuers, Keep Britain Tidy, as an "internationally recognised award that is a benchmark for well-managed green space". As of October 2021, 2227 parks and open spaces held a Green Flag Award.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-GFA-3)

While [public parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_park "Public park") make up most of the awardees, the Green Flag Award is also issued to sites with different uses, such as [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") and [Bluewater Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluewater_Shopping_Centre "Bluewater Shopping Centre"), for the management of their grounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-4)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

The Green Flag Award is managed under licence from the [Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Levelling_Up,_Housing_and_Communities "Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities"), a UK Government department, by [Keep Britain Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Britain_Tidy "Keep Britain Tidy"), which also administers the scheme in England,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-who-5) and several other countries, including Australia and the United States.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-6)

## Accreditation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Accreditation")]

The owners of spaces that wish to hold the accreditation, pay a fee to be assessed by volunteer judges on an annual basis with a process involving [secret shoppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_shopper "Mystery shopper") and inspection of both the park and the owner's management plans. The aspects that spaces are judged on are:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-Guide-7)

1.   A Welcoming Place
2.   Healthy, Safe and Secure
3.   Well Maintained and Clean
4.   Environmental Management
5.   Biodiversity, Landscape and Heritage
6.   Community Involvement
7.   Marketing and Communication
8.   Management

A failure to meet the judges' standards can result in the accreditation being withdrawn; one example of this is North London's [Finsbury Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsbury_Park "Finsbury Park") which lost its Green Flag in 2018.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-8)

The **Green Flag Award** is an international accreditation given to publicly accessible parks and open spaces, managed under licence from the [Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Levelling_Up,_Housing_and_Communities "Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities"), a UK Government department, by [Keep Britain Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Britain_Tidy "Keep Britain Tidy"), which also administers the scheme in England.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Green Flag Award was introduced in 1996, and first awarded in 1997, by the [Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Housing,_Communities_and_Local_Government "Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government") (MHCLG) with the intention of establishing agreed standards of good management, to help to justify and evaluate funding and to raise park attendance. The scheme was managed by [Civic Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Trust_(England) "Civic Trust (England)"), on MHCLG's behalf, until they lost the contract and the charity went bust in 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-1)

The scheme has been managed by Keep Britain Tidy since 2012,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-2) with sister organisations [Keep Scotland Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Scotland_Beautiful "Keep Scotland Beautiful"), [Keep Wales Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Wales_Tidy "Keep Wales Tidy") and [TIDY Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TIDY_Northern_Ireland "TIDY Northern Ireland") delivering the scheme across the UK, and various other bodies delivering worldwide.

## Purpose and description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Purpose and description")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg/250px-Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Flag_on_display_in_Manor_Park.jpg)[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Boscombe_Chine_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg/250px-Boscombe_Chine_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boscombe_Chine_Gardens,_Green_Flag_Award_-_geograph.org.uk_-_619592.jpg)
[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg/250px-Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baysgarth_Park_green_flag.jpg)
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Bournemouth_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg/250px-Bournemouth_Gardens%2C_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bournemouth_Gardens,_Green_Flag_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1702578.jpg)
Green Flags on Display in [Manor Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manor_Park,_London "Manor Park, London"), London; [Boscombe Chine Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe "Boscombe"), Dorset; [Baysgarth Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baysgarth_Park "Baysgarth Park"), Lincolnshire; and [Bournemouth Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth_Gardens,_England "Bournemouth Gardens, England"), Dorset.

The scheme's aim is to promote standards of good management and best-practice amongst the green space sector. It is described by its issuers, Keep Britain Tidy, as an "internationally recognised award that is a benchmark for well-managed green space". As of October 2021, 2227 parks and open spaces held a Green Flag Award.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-GFA-3)

While [public parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_park "Public park") make up most of the awardees, the Green Flag Award is also issued to sites with different uses, such as [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") and [Bluewater Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluewater_Shopping_Centre "Bluewater Shopping Centre"), for the management of their grounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-4)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

The Green Flag Award is managed under licence from the [Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Levelling_Up,_Housing_and_Communities "Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities"), a UK Government department, by [Keep Britain Tidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_Britain_Tidy "Keep Britain Tidy"), which also administers the scheme in England,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-who-5) and several other countries, including Australia and the United States.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-6)

## Accreditation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_Flag_Award&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Accreditation")]

The owners of spaces that wish to hold the accreditation, pay a fee to be assessed by volunteer judges on an annual basis with a process involving [secret shoppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_shopper "Mystery shopper") and inspection of both the park and the owner's management plans. The aspects that spaces are judged on are:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-Guide-7)

1.   A Welcoming Place
2.   Healthy, Safe and Secure
3.   Well Maintained and Clean
4.   Environmental Management
5.   Biodiversity, Landscape and Heritage
6.   Community Involvement
7.   Marketing and Communication
8.   Management

A failure to meet the judges' standards can result in the accreditation being withdrawn; one example of this is North London's [Finsbury Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsbury_Park "Finsbury Park") which lost its Green Flag in 2018.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Flag_Award#cite_note-8)

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**William Gowland**[FRAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Anthropological_Institute_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland") (16 December 1842 – 9 June 1922) was an English mining engineer who carried out [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") work at [Stonehenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge "Stonehenge") and in Japan. He has been called the "Father of Japanese Archaeology".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-1)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Gowland was born in [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland,_Tyne_and_Wear "Sunderland, Tyne and Wear"), County Durham, in northern England. He attended the [Royal College of Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Chemistry "Royal College of Chemistry") and [Royal School of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_School_of_Mines "Royal School of Mines") at [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington "South Kensington"), specialising in [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy"), and worked as a chemist and as a metallurgist at the Broughton Copper Company from 1870 to 1872. However, in 1872, at the age of 30, he was recruited by the [Meiji government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_government "Meiji government") of the [Empire of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") as a [foreign engineering advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-yatoi_gaikokujin "O-yatoi gaikokujin") at the _Osaka Zōheikyoku_, the forerunner of the [Japan Mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Mint "Japan Mint").

## In Japan (1872–88)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: In Japan (1872–88)")]

Gowland began work in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") on 8 October 1872 on the three-year contract that was typical of many of the foreigners employed to aid the modernisation of Japan. His contract was repeatedly extended, and he stayed for 16 years, during which time he introduced techniques for the scientific analysis of metals, the production of [bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze "Bronze") and [copper alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_alloy "Copper alloy") for [coinage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_(coin) "Mint (coin)"), and modern technologies such as the [reverberatory furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberatory_furnace "Reverberatory furnace") for improving the efficiency of [refining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refining "Refining")[copper ores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_ore "Copper ore"). His expertise extended to areas outside the Japan Mint, and he also served as a consultant to the [Imperial Japanese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army"), helping to establish the Osaka Arsenal for production of [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery"). In 1883, he was awarded the [Order of the Rising Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Rising_Sun "Order of the Rising Sun") (4th class) by the Japanese government.

During his spare time in Japan, Gowland enjoyed [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), making the first recorded ascent on several peaks of the [Japanese Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Alps "Japanese Alps"), a name which Gowland coined and which was published in 1888 by [Basil Hall Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Hall_Chamberlain "Basil Hall Chamberlain") in his _Japan Guide_.[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:William\_Gowland#Dubious "Talk:William Gowland")_] The name was later popularised by English missionary [Walter Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Weston "Walter Weston"). Gowland also claimed to have been the first foreigner to have climbed [Yarigatake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Yari "Mount Yari") in 1874.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-2)

However, Gowland is best known in Japan as an amateur [archaeologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeology "Archeology"), conducting the first truly accurate scientific surveys of numerous [Kofun period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun_period "Kofun period") (3rd–7th centuries AD) [burial mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun "Kofun") (_[kofun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun "Kofun")_), which included numerous imperial mausolea. He excavated [burial mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_mounds "Burial mounds") in [Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga_prefecture "Saga prefecture"), [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Prefecture "Fukuoka Prefecture") and [Miyazaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyazaki_prefecture "Miyazaki prefecture") Prefectures on [Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū"), in [Okayama Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okayama_Prefecture "Okayama Prefecture"), and in [Fukushima Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_Prefecture "Fukushima Prefecture") north of Tokyo, in addition to numerous sites in the [Kinki region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinki_region "Kinki region").

Upon Gowland's departure from Japan in 1888, he was awarded the Order of the Rising Sun, 4th class, and a 3,000-yen bonus from then-[Finance Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Japan) "Ministry of Finance (Japan)")[Matsukata Masayoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsukata_Masayoshi "Matsukata Masayoshi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-hkey-3) Once back in England, he published numerous works about his researches in Japan and was elected a Fellow of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society"). He donated many of the artefacts that he brought back to England to the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"), as well as a collection of souvenirs from Buddhist temples.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-4) Gowland was also an avid collector of _[Nihonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihonga "Nihonga")_-style Japanese paintings.

## In England

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: In England")]

On 31 December 1900, Stone 22 of the [Sarsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarsen "Sarsen") Circle fell over during a storm, taking with it a [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel"). Following public pressure and a letter to _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ by [William Flinders Petrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Flinders_Petrie "William Flinders Petrie"), the owner Edmund Antrobus agreed to allow remedial engineering under archaeological supervision. To manage the job, Antrobus appointed Gowland, who, despite having no formal archaeological training, produced some of the finest, most detailed excavation records ever made at the monument. The only area that he opened was around the precariously leaning Stone 56 (the western stone of the Great Trilithon), an area measuring approximately 17 by 13 ft (5.2 by 4.0 m). The task proved more difficult since only small areas could be dug at a time for the pouring and the setting of [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete").

Despite these difficulties, he established that antler picks had been used to dig the stone holes and that the stones had been shaped on site. His work both identified the 'Stonehenge layer', a thin stratum of [bluestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluestone "Bluestone") chips that sealed many of the non-[megalithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalithic "Megalithic") features at the site, and proved that these chips predated the standing stones.

## Final years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Final years")]

Gowland died in London on 9 June 1922 at the age of 79. He was buried at St. Marylebone Cemetery in East Finchley.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-hkey-3)

**William Gowland**[FRAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Anthropological_Institute_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland") (16 December 1842 – 9 June 1922) was an English mining engineer who carried out [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") work at [Stonehenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge "Stonehenge") and in Japan. He has been called the "Father of Japanese Archaeology".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-1)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Gowland was born in [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland,_Tyne_and_Wear "Sunderland, Tyne and Wear"), County Durham, in northern England. He attended the [Royal College of Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Chemistry "Royal College of Chemistry") and [Royal School of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_School_of_Mines "Royal School of Mines") at [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington "South Kensington"), specialising in [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy"), and worked as a chemist and as a metallurgist at the Broughton Copper Company from 1870 to 1872. However, in 1872, at the age of 30, he was recruited by the [Meiji government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_government "Meiji government") of the [Empire of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") as a [foreign engineering advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-yatoi_gaikokujin "O-yatoi gaikokujin") at the _Osaka Zōheikyoku_, the forerunner of the [Japan Mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Mint "Japan Mint").

## In Japan (1872–88)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: In Japan (1872–88)")]

Gowland began work in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") on 8 October 1872 on the three-year contract that was typical of many of the foreigners employed to aid the modernisation of Japan. His contract was repeatedly extended, and he stayed for 16 years, during which time he introduced techniques for the scientific analysis of metals, the production of [bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze "Bronze") and [copper alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_alloy "Copper alloy") for [coinage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_(coin) "Mint (coin)"), and modern technologies such as the [reverberatory furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberatory_furnace "Reverberatory furnace") for improving the efficiency of [refining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refining "Refining")[copper ores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_ore "Copper ore"). His expertise extended to areas outside the Japan Mint, and he also served as a consultant to the [Imperial Japanese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army"), helping to establish the Osaka Arsenal for production of [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery"). In 1883, he was awarded the [Order of the Rising Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Rising_Sun "Order of the Rising Sun") (4th class) by the Japanese government.

During his spare time in Japan, Gowland enjoyed [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), making the first recorded ascent on several peaks of the [Japanese Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Alps "Japanese Alps"), a name which Gowland coined and which was published in 1888 by [Basil Hall Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Hall_Chamberlain "Basil Hall Chamberlain") in his _Japan Guide_.[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:William\_Gowland#Dubious "Talk:William Gowland")_] The name was later popularised by English missionary [Walter Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Weston "Walter Weston"). Gowland also claimed to have been the first foreigner to have climbed [Yarigatake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Yari "Mount Yari") in 1874.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-2)

However, Gowland is best known in Japan as an amateur [archaeologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeology "Archeology"), conducting the first truly accurate scientific surveys of numerous [Kofun period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun_period "Kofun period") (3rd–7th centuries AD) [burial mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun "Kofun") (_[kofun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun "Kofun")_), which included numerous imperial mausolea. He excavated [burial mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_mounds "Burial mounds") in [Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga_prefecture "Saga prefecture"), [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Prefecture "Fukuoka Prefecture") and [Miyazaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyazaki_prefecture "Miyazaki prefecture") Prefectures on [Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū"), in [Okayama Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okayama_Prefecture "Okayama Prefecture"), and in [Fukushima Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_Prefecture "Fukushima Prefecture") north of Tokyo, in addition to numerous sites in the [Kinki region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinki_region "Kinki region").

Upon Gowland's departure from Japan in 1888, he was awarded the Order of the Rising Sun, 4th class, and a 3,000-yen bonus from then-[Finance Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Japan) "Ministry of Finance (Japan)")[Matsukata Masayoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsukata_Masayoshi "Matsukata Masayoshi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-hkey-3) Once back in England, he published numerous works about his researches in Japan and was elected a Fellow of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society"). He donated many of the artefacts that he brought back to England to the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"), as well as a collection of souvenirs from Buddhist temples.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-4) Gowland was also an avid collector of _[Nihonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihonga "Nihonga")_-style Japanese paintings.

## In England

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: In England")]

On 31 December 1900, Stone 22 of the [Sarsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarsen "Sarsen") Circle fell over during a storm, taking with it a [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel"). Following public pressure and a letter to _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ by [William Flinders Petrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Flinders_Petrie "William Flinders Petrie"), the owner Edmund Antrobus agreed to allow remedial engineering under archaeological supervision. To manage the job, Antrobus appointed Gowland, who, despite having no formal archaeological training, produced some of the finest, most detailed excavation records ever made at the monument. The only area that he opened was around the precariously leaning Stone 56 (the western stone of the Great Trilithon), an area measuring approximately 17 by 13 ft (5.2 by 4.0 m). The task proved more difficult since only small areas could be dug at a time for the pouring and the setting of [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete").

Despite these difficulties, he established that antler picks had been used to dig the stone holes and that the stones had been shaped on site. His work both identified the 'Stonehenge layer', a thin stratum of [bluestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluestone "Bluestone") chips that sealed many of the non-[megalithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalithic "Megalithic") features at the site, and proved that these chips predated the standing stones.

## Final years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Gowland&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Final years")]

Gowland died in London on 9 June 1922 at the age of 79. He was buried at St. Marylebone Cemetery in East Finchley.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gowland#cite_note-hkey-3)

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marylebone_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**Highgate Cemetery** is a place of burial in [North London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_London "North London"), England, designed by architect [Stephen Geary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Geary "Stephen Geary").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-1) There are approximately 170,000 people buried in around 53,000 graves across the West and East sides.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-2) Highgate Cemetery is notable both for some of the people buried there either in [coffins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffin "Coffin") or [urns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urn "Urn")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-3) as well as for its _de facto_ status as a [nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_reserve "Nature reserve"). The Cemetery is designated Grade I on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGarden-4)

## Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Location")]

The [cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") is in [Highgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate "Highgate") N6, next to [Waterlow Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterlow_Park "Waterlow Park"), in the [London Borough of Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Camden "London Borough of Camden"). It comprises two sides, on either side of [Swain's Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swain's_Lane "Swain's Lane"). The main gate is on Swain's Lane, just north of Oakshott Avenue. There is another, disused, gate on Chester Road. The nearest public transport ([Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London "Transport for London")) is the C11 bus, Brookfield Park stop, and [Archway tube station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archway_tube_station "Archway tube station").

## History and setting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History and setting")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Highgate_tombs.jpg/250px-Highgate_tombs.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Highgate_tombs.jpg)

Tombs near the Circle of Lebanon crypts at Highgate Cemetery West, London.

The cemetery in its original form–the northwestern wooded area–opened in 1839 by the [London Cemetery Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Cemetery_Company "London Cemetery Company"), as part of a plan to provide seven [large, modern cemeteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_cemetery "Rural cemetery"), now known as the "[Magnificent Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnificent_Seven_cemeteries "Magnificent Seven cemeteries")", around the outside of central London. The inner-city cemeteries, mostly the graveyards attached to individual churches, had long been unable to cope with the number of burials and were seen as a hazard to health and an undignified way to treat the dead. The initial design was by architect and entrepreneur [Stephen Geary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Geary "Stephen Geary"). The London Cemetery Company was incorporated by the [London Cemetery Company Act 1836](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Cemetery_Company_Act_1836 "London Cemetery Company Act 1836") ([6 & 7 Will. 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6_&_7_Will._4 "6 & 7 Will. 4"). c. cxxxvi).

On 20 May 1839, Highgate (West) Cemetery was dedicated to [St James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James,_son_of_Alphaeus "James, son of Alphaeus")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-5) by the Right Reverend [Charles James Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_James_Blomfield "Charles James Blomfield"), Lord [Bishop of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_London "Bishop of London"). 15 acres (6.1 ha) were consecrated for the use of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), and two acres were set aside for [dissenters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Dissenters "English Dissenters"). Rights of burial were sold either for a limited period or in perpetuity. The first burial was Elizabeth Jackson of Little Windmill Street, [Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho "Soho"), on 26 May.

Highgate, like the others of the Magnificent Seven, soon became a fashionable place for burials and was much admired and visited. The [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") attitude to death and its presentation[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] led to the creation of a wealth of [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") tombs and buildings. It occupies a spectacular south-facing hillside site slightly downhill from the top of Highgate hill, next to Waterlow Park. In 1854 a further 19 acres (8 ha) to the south east of the original area, across Swain's Lane, were bought to form the eastern extension; this opened in 1860. Both sides of the cemetery are still used today for burials.

The cemetery's grounds are full of trees, shrubbery and wildflowers, most of which have been planted and grown without human influence.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] The grounds are a haven for birds and small mammals, such as foxes. The London Cemetery Company became bankrupt in 1960, and was absorbed by the United Cemetery Company. The cemetery is now owned and maintained by a charitable trust, the Friends of Highgate Cemetery Trust, which was set up in 1975 and acquired the freehold of both East and West sides by 1981. In 1984 it published _Highgate Cemetery: Victorian Valhalla_ by [John Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gay_(photographer) "John Gay (photographer)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-6) The trust was given updated powers to manage the cemetery and extinguish rights of burial by the **Highgate Cemetery Act 2022** (c. i).

## Graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Graves")]

### West Side

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: West Side")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg/250px-Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg)

Entrance to the Egyptian Avenue, Highgate Cemetery West

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/High-cemetery-circle.jpg/250px-High-cemetery-circle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:High-cemetery-circle.jpg)

Circle of Lebanon, Highgate Cemetery West

The Egyptian Avenue and the Circle of Lebanon (previously surmounted by a huge, 280-year-old [Cedar of Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar"), which had to be cut down and replaced in August 2019) are both Grade I [listed buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_buildings "Listed buildings"). The west side of the Cemetery is characterised by elaborate feature tombs, vaults and winding paths dug into hillsides. At the highest point, the Terrace [Catacombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs "Catacombs") and the [Julius Beer Mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Beer_Mausoleum "Julius Beer Mausoleum") are both Grade II* listed. In 1967 the Dissenter's Catacombs were declared unsafe and demolished. Three houses were subsequently built on the site. [The Grey House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grey_House,_Highgate "The Grey House, Highgate"), built in 2008, is visible from the West Side of the cemetery on Faraday Path.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-Highgate22-7)

Many famous or prominent people are buried on this side of Highgate cemetery; the most famous of which is perhaps that of [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx"), whose tomb was the site of attempted bombings on 2 September 1965[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-11) and in 1970.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-12) The [tomb of Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Karl_Marx "Tomb of Karl Marx") is also a Grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") for reasons of historical importance. Fireman's corner is a monument erected in the East side by widows and orphans of members of the [London Fire Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Fire_Brigade "London Fire Brigade") in 1934. There are 97 firemen buried here. The monument is cared for by the Brigade's Welfare Section.

### War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: War graves")]

The cemetery contains the graves of 318 Commonwealth service personnel maintained and registered by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission"), in both the East and West sides, 259 from the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") and 59 from the [Second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). Those whose graves could not be marked by headstones are listed on a Screen Wall memorial erected near the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice") in the west side.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgc-15)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Highgate Cemetery was featured in the popular media from the 1960s to the late 1980s for its so-called [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult") past, particularly as being the alleged site of the "[Highgate Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Vampire "Highgate Vampire")".

*   Several of [John Galsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Galsworthy "John Galsworthy")'s _[Forsyte Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Forsyte\_Saga "The Forsyte Saga")_ novels refer to Highgate Cemetery as the last resting place of the Forsytes; for example, Chapter XI, "The Last of the Forsytes", in _To Let_ (1921).
*   Footage of Highgate appears in numerous British horror films, including _[Taste the Blood of Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste\_the\_Blood\_of\_Dracula "Taste the Blood of Dracula")_ (1970), _[Tales from the Crypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_the\_Crypt\_(film) "Tales from the Crypt (film)")_ (1972) and _[From Beyond the Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Beyond\_the\_Grave "From Beyond the Grave")_ (1974).
*   In _[That's Your Funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_Your\_Funeral "That's Your Funeral")_ (1972), the route taken in the Hearse Drivers' Grand Prix is mentioned as going "from [Golders Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golders_Green_Crematorium "Golders Green Crematorium") to [Woking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Crematorium "Woking Crematorium") via [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx")'s grave in Highgate".
*   In [Len Deighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Len_Deighton "Len Deighton")'s alternative history novel _[SS-GB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS-GB "SS-GB")_ and its [TV adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS-GB_(TV_series) "SS-GB (TV series)"), a bomb is detonated in the tomb of [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx") when his remains are exhumed by [German occupation forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") to be presented to the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").
*   [Audrey Niffenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audrey_Niffenegger "Audrey Niffenegger")'s book _[Her Fearful Symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her\_Fearful\_Symmetry "Her Fearful Symmetry")_ (2009) is set around Highgate Cemetery; she acted as a tour guide there while researching the book.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-Highgate_Cemetery-16)
*   In the novel _[Double or Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double\_or\_Die "Double or Die")_ (2007), a part of the _[Young Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Bond "Young Bond")_ series, Ludwig and Wolfgang Smith plan to kill Bond in the cemetery.
*   [Tracy Chevalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Chevalier "Tracy Chevalier")'s book _Falling Angels_ (2002) was set in and around Highgate Cemetery.
*   The film [_Hampstead_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_(film) "Hampstead (film)") (2017) features some scenes in the cemetery.
*   [Robert Galbraith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._K._Rowling "J. K. Rowling")'s sixth [Cormoran Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cormoran_Strike "Cormoran Strike") novel _[The Ink Black Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ink\_Black\_Heart "The Ink Black Heart")_ (2022) revolves around a fictional cartoon set in Highgate Cemetery.

**Highgate Cemetery** is a place of burial in [North London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_London "North London"), England, designed by architect [Stephen Geary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Geary "Stephen Geary").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-1) There are approximately 170,000 people buried in around 53,000 graves across the West and East sides.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-2) Highgate Cemetery is notable both for some of the people buried there either in [coffins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffin "Coffin") or [urns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urn "Urn")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-3) as well as for its _de facto_ status as a [nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_reserve "Nature reserve"). The Cemetery is designated Grade I on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLEGarden-4)

## Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Location")]

The [cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") is in [Highgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate "Highgate") N6, next to [Waterlow Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterlow_Park "Waterlow Park"), in the [London Borough of Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Camden "London Borough of Camden"). It comprises two sides, on either side of [Swain's Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swain's_Lane "Swain's Lane"). The main gate is on Swain's Lane, just north of Oakshott Avenue. There is another, disused, gate on Chester Road. The nearest public transport ([Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London "Transport for London")) is the C11 bus, Brookfield Park stop, and [Archway tube station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archway_tube_station "Archway tube station").

## History and setting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History and setting")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Highgate_tombs.jpg/250px-Highgate_tombs.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Highgate_tombs.jpg)

Tombs near the Circle of Lebanon crypts at Highgate Cemetery West, London.

The cemetery in its original form–the northwestern wooded area–opened in 1839 by the [London Cemetery Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Cemetery_Company "London Cemetery Company"), as part of a plan to provide seven [large, modern cemeteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_cemetery "Rural cemetery"), now known as the "[Magnificent Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnificent_Seven_cemeteries "Magnificent Seven cemeteries")", around the outside of central London. The inner-city cemeteries, mostly the graveyards attached to individual churches, had long been unable to cope with the number of burials and were seen as a hazard to health and an undignified way to treat the dead. The initial design was by architect and entrepreneur [Stephen Geary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Geary "Stephen Geary"). The London Cemetery Company was incorporated by the [London Cemetery Company Act 1836](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Cemetery_Company_Act_1836 "London Cemetery Company Act 1836") ([6 & 7 Will. 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6_&_7_Will._4 "6 & 7 Will. 4"). c. cxxxvi).

On 20 May 1839, Highgate (West) Cemetery was dedicated to [St James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James,_son_of_Alphaeus "James, son of Alphaeus")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-5) by the Right Reverend [Charles James Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_James_Blomfield "Charles James Blomfield"), Lord [Bishop of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_London "Bishop of London"). 15 acres (6.1 ha) were consecrated for the use of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), and two acres were set aside for [dissenters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Dissenters "English Dissenters"). Rights of burial were sold either for a limited period or in perpetuity. The first burial was Elizabeth Jackson of Little Windmill Street, [Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho "Soho"), on 26 May.

Highgate, like the others of the Magnificent Seven, soon became a fashionable place for burials and was much admired and visited. The [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") attitude to death and its presentation[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] led to the creation of a wealth of [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") tombs and buildings. It occupies a spectacular south-facing hillside site slightly downhill from the top of Highgate hill, next to Waterlow Park. In 1854 a further 19 acres (8 ha) to the south east of the original area, across Swain's Lane, were bought to form the eastern extension; this opened in 1860. Both sides of the cemetery are still used today for burials.
