The cemetery's grounds are full of trees, shrubbery and wildflowers, most of which have been planted and grown without human influence.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] The grounds are a haven for birds and small mammals, such as foxes. The London Cemetery Company became bankrupt in 1960, and was absorbed by the United Cemetery Company. The cemetery is now owned and maintained by a charitable trust, the Friends of Highgate Cemetery Trust, which was set up in 1975 and acquired the freehold of both East and West sides by 1981. In 1984 it published _Highgate Cemetery: Victorian Valhalla_ by [John Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gay_(photographer) "John Gay (photographer)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-6) The trust was given updated powers to manage the cemetery and extinguish rights of burial by the **Highgate Cemetery Act 2022** (c. i).

## Graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Graves")]

### West Side

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: West Side")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg/250px-Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Egyptian_Avenue_Highgate_Cemetery.jpg)

Entrance to the Egyptian Avenue, Highgate Cemetery West

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/High-cemetery-circle.jpg/250px-High-cemetery-circle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:High-cemetery-circle.jpg)

Circle of Lebanon, Highgate Cemetery West

The Egyptian Avenue and the Circle of Lebanon (previously surmounted by a huge, 280-year-old [Cedar of Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar"), which had to be cut down and replaced in August 2019) are both Grade I [listed buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_buildings "Listed buildings"). The west side of the Cemetery is characterised by elaborate feature tombs, vaults and winding paths dug into hillsides. At the highest point, the Terrace [Catacombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs "Catacombs") and the [Julius Beer Mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Beer_Mausoleum "Julius Beer Mausoleum") are both Grade II* listed. In 1967 the Dissenter's Catacombs were declared unsafe and demolished. Three houses were subsequently built on the site. [The Grey House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grey_House,_Highgate "The Grey House, Highgate"), built in 2008, is visible from the West Side of the cemetery on Faraday Path.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-Highgate22-7)

Many famous or prominent people are buried on this side of Highgate cemetery; the most famous of which is perhaps that of [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx"), whose tomb was the site of attempted bombings on 2 September 1965[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-11) and in 1970.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-12) The [tomb of Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Karl_Marx "Tomb of Karl Marx") is also a Grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") for reasons of historical importance. Fireman's corner is a monument erected in the East side by widows and orphans of members of the [London Fire Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Fire_Brigade "London Fire Brigade") in 1934. There are 97 firemen buried here. The monument is cared for by the Brigade's Welfare Section.

### War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: War graves")]

The cemetery contains the graves of 318 Commonwealth service personnel maintained and registered by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission"), in both the East and West sides, 259 from the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") and 59 from the [Second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). Those whose graves could not be marked by headstones are listed on a Screen Wall memorial erected near the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice") in the west side.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgc-15)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Highgate_Cemetery&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Highgate Cemetery was featured in the popular media from the 1960s to the late 1980s for its so-called [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult") past, particularly as being the alleged site of the "[Highgate Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Vampire "Highgate Vampire")".

*   Several of [John Galsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Galsworthy "John Galsworthy")'s _[Forsyte Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Forsyte\_Saga "The Forsyte Saga")_ novels refer to Highgate Cemetery as the last resting place of the Forsytes; for example, Chapter XI, "The Last of the Forsytes", in _To Let_ (1921).
*   Footage of Highgate appears in numerous British horror films, including _[Taste the Blood of Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste\_the\_Blood\_of\_Dracula "Taste the Blood of Dracula")_ (1970), _[Tales from the Crypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_the\_Crypt\_(film) "Tales from the Crypt (film)")_ (1972) and _[From Beyond the Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Beyond\_the\_Grave "From Beyond the Grave")_ (1974).
*   In _[That's Your Funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_Your\_Funeral "That's Your Funeral")_ (1972), the route taken in the Hearse Drivers' Grand Prix is mentioned as going "from [Golders Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golders_Green_Crematorium "Golders Green Crematorium") to [Woking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Crematorium "Woking Crematorium") via [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx")'s grave in Highgate".
*   In [Len Deighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Len_Deighton "Len Deighton")'s alternative history novel _[SS-GB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS-GB "SS-GB")_ and its [TV adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS-GB_(TV_series) "SS-GB (TV series)"), a bomb is detonated in the tomb of [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx") when his remains are exhumed by [German occupation forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") to be presented to the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").
*   [Audrey Niffenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audrey_Niffenegger "Audrey Niffenegger")'s book _[Her Fearful Symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her\_Fearful\_Symmetry "Her Fearful Symmetry")_ (2009) is set around Highgate Cemetery; she acted as a tour guide there while researching the book.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_Cemetery#cite_note-Highgate_Cemetery-16)
*   In the novel _[Double or Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double\_or\_Die "Double or Die")_ (2007), a part of the _[Young Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Bond "Young Bond")_ series, Ludwig and Wolfgang Smith plan to kill Bond in the cemetery.
*   [Tracy Chevalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Chevalier "Tracy Chevalier")'s book _Falling Angels_ (2002) was set in and around Highgate Cemetery.
*   The film [_Hampstead_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_(film) "Hampstead (film)") (2017) features some scenes in the cemetery.
*   [Robert Galbraith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._K._Rowling "J. K. Rowling")'s sixth [Cormoran Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cormoran_Strike "Cormoran Strike") novel _[The Ink Black Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ink\_Black\_Heart "The Ink Black Heart")_ (2022) revolves around a fictional cartoon set in Highgate Cemetery.

**Brookwood Cemetery**, also known as the **London Necropolis**, is a burial ground in [Brookwood, Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood,_Surrey "Brookwood, Surrey"), England. It is the largest cemetery in the United Kingdom and one of the largest in Europe. The cemetery is listed a Grade I site in the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLE-9)

The [Church of St Edward the Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St_Edward_the_Martyr,_Brookwood "Church of St Edward the Martyr, Brookwood") with its community of [Greek Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Orthodox_Church "Greek Orthodox Church") monks is located in the cemetery grounds.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

Brookwood Cemetery was conceived by the [London Necropolis Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_Company "London Necropolis Company") (LNC) in 1849 to house [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")'s deceased, at a time when the capital was finding it difficult to accommodate its increasing population, both living and dead. The cemetery is said to have been landscaped by [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect")[William Tite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tite "William Tite"), but this is disputed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-10)

Brookwood Cemetery's initial owner was incorporated by Act of Parliament in 1852, and the cemetery was consecrated by [Charles Sumner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sumner_(bishop) "Charles Sumner (bishop)"), [Bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"), on 7 November 1854 (apart from its northern section, reserved for Nonconformists). It was opened to the public on 13 November 1854 when the first burials took place. It was the largest [cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") in the world in 1854, but has since lost that distinction.

In 1857 actor [John W. Anson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_W._Anson "John W. Anson") acquired 1 acre (4,000 m 2) of land there, the Actors' Acre, for the 'Dramatic, Equestrian and Musical Sick Fund Association' as a burial place for actors and their relatives.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-11)

In 1858 the London Necropolis Company sold 64 acres (26 ha) of the extra land to the government for the building of [Woking Convict Invalid Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Convict_Invalid_Prison "Woking Convict Invalid Prison").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-12)

### Necropolis Railway

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Necropolis Railway")]

Main article: [London Necropolis Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_Railway "London Necropolis Railway")

Brookwood originally was accessible by rail from a special station – the [London Necropolis railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_railway_station "London Necropolis railway station") – next to [Waterloo station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Waterloo_station "London Waterloo station") in Central London. Trains had passenger carriages reserved for different classes and other carriages for coffins (also for different classes), and ran into the cemetery on a dedicated branch from the adjoining [South West Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Main_Line "South West Main Line") – there was a junction just to the west of [Brookwood station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_railway_station "Brookwood railway station"). From there, passengers and coffins were transported by [horse-drawn vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse-drawn_vehicles "Horse-drawn vehicles"). The original London Necropolis station was relocated in 1902 but its successor was demolished after suffering bomb damage during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

[![Image 7: Railway ticket labelled "Southern Railways London Necropolis Coffin Ticket, Waterloo to Brookwood, Third Class](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/d/dd/Brookwood_Coffin_Ticket.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_Coffin_Ticket.jpg)

Third class coffin ticket, issued between April–September 1925.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006162-13)

Return tickets were issued for mourners and single tickets for the dead.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006150-14)

There were two stations in the cemetery: _North_ for non-conformists and _South_ for Anglicans. Their platforms still exist along the path called Railway Avenue. For visitors wishing to use the South West Main Line, Brookwood station has provided direct access since June 1864. A very short piece of commemorative track, with signpost and plaque, purposefully gives way to a grass field and recollects the old final stage of the journey of the deceased.

It was the cholera epidemic of 1848 that led two industrialists to develop this high burial site. It was at first a controversial project. The Bishop of London condemned the "offensive" despatch of first-, second- and third-class corpses in the same carriages, so this had to be modified.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Early burials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early burials")]

The LNC offered three classes of funerals:

*   A first class funeral allowed buyers to select the grave site of their choice anywhere in the cemetery. The LNC charged extra for burials in some designated special sites.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15) At the time of opening prices began at £2 10[s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling_(British_coin) "Shilling (British coin)") (about £240 in 2025 terms) for a basic 9-by-4-foot (2.7 m ×1.2 m) with no special coffin specifications.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-inflation-UK-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15) It was expected by the LNC that those using first class graves would erect a permanent memorial of some kind in due course following the funeral.
*   Second class funerals cost £1 (about £96 in 2025 terms) and allowed some control over the burial location.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200681-17) The right to erect a permanent memorial cost an additional 10 [shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling_(British_coin) "Shilling (British coin)") (about £48 in 2025 terms); if a permanent memorial was not erected the LNC reserved the right to re-use the grave in future.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-inflation-UK-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15)
*   Third class funerals were reserved for pauper funerals; those buried at [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish") expense in the section of the cemetery designated for that parish. Although the LNC was forbidden from using mass graves (other than the burial of next of kin in the same grave) and thus even the lowest class of funeral provided a separate grave for the deceased, third class funerals were not granted the right to erect a permanent memorial on the site.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200681-17) (The families of those buried could pay afterwards to upgrade a third class grave to a higher class if they later wanted to erect a memorial, but this practice was rare.)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200416-18) Despite this, Brookwood's pauper graves granted more dignity to the deceased than did other graveyards and cemeteries of the period, all of which other than Brookwood continued the practice of mass graves for the poor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006103-19)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg/250px-Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg)

The monument to [Sir Henry Goldfinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Goldfinch "Henry Goldfinch") is the earliest in the cemetery. Brookwood Columbarian in background left.

Brookwood was one of the few cemeteries to permit burials on Sundays, which made it a popular choice with the poor as it allowed people to attend funerals without the need to take a day off work.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200691-20) As theatrical performances were banned on Sundays at this time, it also made Brookwood a popular choice for the burial of actors for the same reason, to the extent that actors were provided with a dedicated section of the cemetery near the station entrance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006103-19)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200693-21)

While the majority of burials conducted by the LNC (around 80%) were pauper funerals on behalf of London parishes and prisons,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200416-18) the LNC also reached agreement with a number of societies, guilds, religious bodies and similar organisations (such as [Woking Convict Invalid Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Convict_Invalid_Prison "Woking Convict Invalid Prison") and [Tothill Fields House of Correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tothill_Fields_Bridewell "Tothill Fields Bridewell")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-22)). The LNC provided dedicated sections of the cemetery for these groups, on the basis that those who had lived or worked together in life could remain together after death.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200415%E2%80%9316-23) Although the LNC was never able to gain the domination of London's funeral industry for which its founders had hoped, it was very successful at targeting specialist groups of artisans and trades, to the extent that it became nicknamed "the Westminster Abbey of the middle classes".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200420-24) The [Royal Hospital Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Hospital_Chelsea "Royal Hospital Chelsea"), which previously buried their inmate pensioners at [Brompton Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brompton_Cemetery "Brompton Cemetery") in Chelsea, have used Brookwood Cemetery, where they have two plots, since 1893.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-Philpot2018-25)

A large number of these dedicated plots were established, ranging from [Chelsea Pensioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Pensioners "Chelsea Pensioners") and the [Ancient Order of Foresters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Order_of_Foresters "Ancient Order of Foresters") to the [Corps of Commissionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corps_of_Commissionaires "Corps of Commissionaires") and the LSWR.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200415-26) The Nonconformist cemetery also includes a [Parsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsee "Parsee") burial ground established in 1862, which as of 2011[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit) remained the only [Zoroastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrianism "Zoroastrianism") burial ground in Europe.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2004233-27) Dedicated sections in the Anglican cemetery were also reserved for burials from those parishes which had made burial arrangements with the LNC.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28)

The first burial was of the [stillborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stillbirth "Stillbirth") twins of a Mr and Mrs Hore of Ewer Street, [The Borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Borough,_London "The Borough, London").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) The Hore twins, along with the other burials on the first day, were pauper funerals and buried in unmarked graves.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) The first burial at Brookwood with a permanent memorial was that of Lieutenant-General [Sir Henry Goldfinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Goldfinch "Henry Goldfinch"), buried on 25 November 1854, the 26th person to be buried in the cemetery.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413%E2%80%9314-30) The first permanent memorial erected in the Nonconformist section of the cemetery was that of Charles Milligan Hogg, son of botanist [Robert Hogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hogg_(biologist) "Robert Hogg (biologist)"), buried on 12 December 1854.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200414-31) Goldfinch and Hogg's graves are not the oldest monuments in the cemetery, as on occasion gravestones were relocated and re-erected during the relocation of existing burial grounds to Brookwood.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006112-32)

[![Image 9: Grassy area lined with giant sequoia trees, with occasional scattered gravestones](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg/250px-Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg)

The rate of burials was much lower than anticipated by the London Necropolis Company and around 80% of graves are unmarked, making Brookwood distinctively uncluttered when compared to other cemeteries.

Over 235,000 people have been buried there.

### Reburials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reburials")]

The massive London civil engineering projects of the mid-19th century—the railways, the [sewer system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_sewerage_system "London sewerage system") and from the 1860s the precursors to the [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground")—often necessitated the demolition of existing churchyards.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006111-33) The first major relocation took place in 1862, when the construction of [Charing Cross railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross_railway_station "Charing Cross railway station") and the routes into it necessitated the demolition of the burial ground of Cure's College in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), which uncovered at least 7,950 bodies.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006111-33) These were packed into 220 large containers, each containing 26 adults plus children, and shipped on the London Necropolis Railway to Brookwood for reburial, along with at least some of the existing headstones from the cemetery.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006112-32)

At least 21 London burial grounds were relocated to Brookwood via the railway, along with numerous others relocated by road following the railway's closure. Churches whose graves were relocated included:

*   [St Michael, Crooked Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael,_Crooked_Lane "St Michael, Crooked Lane") (demolished 1831, burial ground cleared 1987)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-34)
*   [St Antholin, Budge Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Antholin,_Budge_Row "St Antholin, Budge Row") (demolished 1875)
*   [All-Hallows-the-Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Hallows-the-Great "All-Hallows-the-Great") (demolished 1894)
*   [St Magnus-the-Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Magnus-the-Martyr "St Magnus-the-Martyr") (remains removed from crypt 1894)
*   [All-Hallows-the-Less](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Hallows-the-Less "All-Hallows-the-Less") (destroyed in the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London"), remains removed 1896)
*   [St Michael Wood Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael_Wood_Street "St Michael Wood Street") (demolished 1897)
*   [St Mildred, Bread Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mildred,_Bread_Street "St Mildred, Bread Street") (remains removed 1898, church destroyed in [London Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Blitz "London Blitz") 1941)
*   [St George the Martyr, Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George_the_Martyr,_Southwark "St George the Martyr, Southwark") (remains removed 1899)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-35)
*   [St George Botolph Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George_Botolph_Lane "St George Botolph Lane") (demolished 1904)
*   [St Peter's Church, Eaton Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Peter's_Church,_Eaton_Square "St Peter's Church, Eaton Square") (crypt cleared 1951)
*   [St Marylebone Parish Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Marylebone_Parish_Church "St Marylebone Parish Church") (remains from crypt removed 1987)
*   [St Luke Old Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Luke_Old_Street "St Luke Old Street") (closed 1959, remains from crypt removed 2000)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-36)
*   [St James's Church, Piccadilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly "St James's Church, Piccadilly") (remains removed from St. James's Garden, established 1878 on the former burial grounds of the church, from 2017–2020 due to [HS2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HS2 "HS2") terminal construction at [Euston Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euston_Station "Euston Station")) - the largest exhumation in British history.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-37)
*   The unconsecrated [Cross Bones Graveyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Bones_Graveyard "Cross Bones Graveyard") in Southwark (closed 1853, many remains removed in successive years)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-38)

### Brookwood Cemetery and cremation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Brookwood Cemetery and cremation")]

In 1878, the LNC sold an isolated piece of its land at Brookwood, close to [St John's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's,_Woking "St John's, Woking") village, to the [Cremation Society of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremation_Society_of_Great_Britain "Cremation Society of Great Britain"), on which they built [Woking Crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Crematorium "Woking Crematorium"), the first in Britain, in 1879.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200418-39) While the LNC never built its own crematorium, in 1910, [Lord Cadogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cadogan,_5th_Earl_Cadogan "George Cadogan, 5th Earl Cadogan") decided he no longer wanted to be interred in the mausoleum he had commissioned at Brookwood. This building, the largest mausoleum in the cemetery, was bought by the LNC, fitted with shelves and niches to hold urns, and used as a dedicated [columbarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbarium "Columbarium") from then on.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200424-40)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg/250px-Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg)

Brookwood Columbarium, built as a mausoleum for Lord Cadogan but converted in 1910 for the storage of cremation urns

After 1945 cremation, up to that time an uncommon practice, became increasingly popular in Britain.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2004250-41) In 1946, the LNC obtained consent to build their own crematorium on a section of the Nonconformist cemetery which had been set aside for pauper burials, but chose not to proceed.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42) Instead, in 1945, the LNC began the construction of the Glades of Remembrance, a wooded area dedicated to the burial of cremated remains.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42) These were dedicated by [Henry Montgomery Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Montgomery_Campbell "Henry Montgomery Campbell"), [Bishop of Guildford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Guildford "Bishop of Guildford") in 1950.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-43) Intentionally designed for informality, traditional gravestones and memorials were prohibited, and burials were marked only by small 2-to-3-inch (5.1 to 7.6 cm) stones.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200429-44)

In the next decade, the cemetery came closest to having its own crematorium. Following the closure of the two Brookwood railway stations, the land surrounding the site of South station and the station's two Anglican chapels was redundant. As part of the  ([4 & 5 Eliz. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_&_5_Eliz._2 "4 & 5 Eliz. 2"). c. lxviii), the LNC obtained parliamentary consent to convert the disused original Anglican chapel into a crematorium, using the newer chapel for funeral services and the station building for coffin storage and as a refreshment room for those attending cremations.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200430-45) Suffering cash flow problems and distracted by a succession of hostile takeover bids, the LNC management never proceeded with the scheme and the buildings fell into disuse.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200430-45) The station building was demolished after being damaged by a fire in 1972, although the platform remained intact.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200669-46)

### Horticultural

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Horticultural")]

With the ambition for it to become London's sole burial site in perpetuity, the LNC were aware that if their plans were successful, their Necropolis would become a site of major national importance.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) As a consequence, the cemetery was designed with attractiveness in mind, in contrast to the squalid and congested London burial grounds and the newer suburban cemeteries which were already becoming crowded.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-Times-47)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29)

The LNC aimed to create an atmosphere of perpetual spring in the cemetery, and chose the plants for the cemetery accordingly. It had already been noted that [evergreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen "Evergreen") plants from North America thrived in the local soil.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28) Robert Donald, the owner of an [arboretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboretum "Arboretum") near Woking, was contracted to supply the trees and shrubs for the cemetery.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200410%E2%80%9311-48) The railway line through the cemetery and the major roads and paths within the cemetery were lined with [giant sequoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoiadendron_giganteum "Sequoiadendron giganteum") trees, the first significant planting of these trees (only introduced to Europe in 1853) in Britain.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28) As well as the giant sequoias (also known as _Wellingtonia_ after the recently deceased [Duke of Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington "Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington")), the grounds were heavily planted with [magnolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnolia "Magnolia"), [rhododendron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhododendron "Rhododendron"), [coastal redwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_sempervirens "Sequoia sempervirens"), [azalea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azalea "Azalea"), [andromeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieris_(plant) "Pieris (plant)") and [monkeypuzzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araucaria_araucana "Araucaria araucana"), with the intention of creating perpetual greenery with large numbers of flowers and a strong floral scent throughout the cemetery.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28)

In later years the original planting of the cemetery was supplemented by numerous other tree species planted by the LNC, as well as many plants planted by mourners at burial sites and around mausolea. Between the end of LNC independence in 1959 and the cemetery's purchase by [Ramadan Güney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramadan_G%C3%BCney "Ramadan Güney") in 1985 cemetery maintenance was drastically reduced, and the spread of various plant types caused many of the non-military sections of the cemetery to revert to wilderness in this period.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200431-49)

### 20th and 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 20th and 21st centuries")]

In August 1914, on the outbreak of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), the LNC offered to donate to the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office")1 acre (4,000 m 2) of land "for the free interment of soldiers and sailors who have returned from the front wounded and may subsequently die". The offer was not taken up until 1917, when a section of the cemetery was set aside as Brookwood Military Cemetery, used for the burials of service personnel who died in the [London District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_District_(British_Army) "London District (British Army)").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200424-40) This purpose built cemetery came to accommodate further dead from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

In the meantime, 141 Commonwealth service personnel were buried from London in scattered graves throughout the cemetery, apart from a small Nurses' Plot in St Peter's Avenue in the Westminster field (where are buried nurses from [Millbank Military Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Alexandra_Military_Hospital "Queen Alexandra Military Hospital")) and an Indian plot (including one unidentified soldier) in the North-West corner.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgcbc-50)

In World War II 51 Commonwealth service personnel were buried in the civilian cemetery, where there are also buried five foreign national servicemen whose graves the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") (CWGC) additionally care for.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgcbc-50) A military memorial to the missing from that war was built in 1958 by the CWGC.

[Edward the Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Martyr "Edward the Martyr"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-51) King of England, was memorialised here. His relics are kept nearby in [St Edward the Martyr Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Edward_the_Martyr_Orthodox_Church "St Edward the Martyr Orthodox Church").

The London Necropolis Company was taken over by Alliance Property in 1959[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200631-52) and the company was gradually divested of land and investments until by 1973, the cemetery was an independent entity. The cemetery changed hands between various development companies in the 1970s, during which time the cemetery maintenance was neglected: 1970 Cornwall Property (Holdings) Ltd, 1971 Great Southern Group, 1973 Maximillian Investments.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200631%E2%80%9332-53) Maximillian Investments secured the passing of the **Brookwood Cemetery Act 1975** (c. xxxv) which authorised them to sell unused parts of the cemetery[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200632-54) and a few areas were sold for development.

In 1985, Ramadan Güney acquired Brookwood Cemetery from the owner Mr D. J. T. Dally, who was previously the cemetery manager.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200635-7) The purchase evolved from Güney's role as Chairman of the UK Turkish Islamic Trust, which wanted suitable burial facilities for its members.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-BrookwoodCemetery-6) The Brookwood Cemetery Society was founded in 1992 to organise events, promote the site's history and support restoration work. After Güney's death in 2006 he was buried in the cemetery and ownership passed to his children (by his late wife) and operated by his son Erkin, a director at the cemetery for almost 30 years. Diane Holliday, Güney's partner of 6 years, was "frozen out" from the operating company and then dismissed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DecisionUpheld-4) In 2011, the inheritance of the cemetery was successfully challenged by Diane Holliday and her adult son Kevin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DisputeResolved-5) This decision was upheld by the High Court on appeal in 2012.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DecisionUpheld-4) In 2014, Diane Holliday sold the cemetery to [Woking Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_(borough) "Woking (borough)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-council-3)

In 2017, work began on the exhumation of the remains of approximately 40,000 to 50,000 people who were interred at the [former burial ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly#Detached_burial_ground "St James's Church, Piccadilly") of [St. James's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly "St James's Church, Piccadilly")[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-55) due to construction of the new [HS2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HS2 "HS2") terminal at [Euston Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euston_Station "Euston Station") in London.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-stjameshs2-56) The former burial ground had been in use between 1790 and 1853 before the cemetery became St James's Gardens in 1878. The grounds had been utilised as public park space until they were closed in 2017 at the outset of construction.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-stjameshs2-56) A large part of the exhumation project consisted of a multi-year cataloguing and study of the remains by [osteo-archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoarchaeology "Osteoarchaeology"), part of which was documented by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-57) In 2020 it was announced that it had been agreed by the Woking Council and HS2 that the remains were to be re-interred in a new grassland plot on the south side of Brookwood Cemetery.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-58) The exhumations and study began in October 2018 and the re-interment at Brookwood took place sometime around August 2020 to November 2020.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-clarke-59) At around 50,000 individual remains, it is thought to be the largest single reburial project in the history of Brookwood.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-clarke-59)

## Brookwood Military Cemetery and memorials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Brookwood Military Cemetery and memorials")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG/330px-The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG)

The Brookwood Memorial, built in 1958 and designed by [Ralph Hobday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Hobday "Ralph Hobday")

**Brookwood Military Cemetery** covers about 37 acres (15 ha) and is the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the United Kingdom. The land was set aside during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") to provide a burial site for men and women of Commonwealth and American armed forces who died in the United Kingdom of wounds and other causes. It now contains 1,601 Commonwealth burials from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 3,476 from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (the latter including 3 unidentified [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") and 2 unidentified [Canadian airmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Air_Force "Royal Canadian Air Force")).

Within this, there is a particularly large Canadian section, which includes 43 men who died of wounds following the [Dieppe Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieppe_Raid "Dieppe Raid") in August 1942. Two dozen Muslim dead were also later transferred here in 1968 from the [Muslim Burial Ground at Horsell Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Burial_Ground,_Horsell_Common "Muslim Burial Ground, Horsell Common"). There is a large [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") section in the southeast corner of the cemetery which includes graves of Czech and United States nationals who died serving in the RAF.

The cemetery also has 786 non-Commonwealth war graves, including 28 unidentified French, besides eight German dead from World War I and 46 from World War II.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-60) It also contains Polish (84 graves), Czech, Belgian (46 graves), Dutch (seven graves) and Italian (over 300 graves) sections.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-61) Except for [Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day "Christmas Day") and [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day"), this cemetery is open to the public from 8am to sunset Monday to Friday, and 9am to sunset Saturdays and Sundays.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-62)

The **Brookwood 1914–1918 Memorial** originally stood at the northeastern end of the 1914–1918 Plot. The new memorial that replaced it was created in 2004, and currently (23 June 2025) commemorates 391 Commonwealth service personnel who died in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") in the United Kingdom but have no known grave. The majority of the casualties commemorated on the Brookwood 1914–1918 Memorial are servicemen and women identified by the In From The Cold Project as having died while in care of their families and were not commemorated by the Commission at the time. (Those whose graves are subsequently discovered become commemorated under the respective cemetery.)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-63)

The **Brookwood 1939-1945 Memorial** stands at the southern end of the Canadian section of the cemetery and commemorates 3,428 Commonwealth men and women who died during the Second World War and have no known grave. This includes commandos killed in the [Dieppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieppe_Raid "Dieppe Raid") and [St Nazaire Raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Nazaire_Raid "St Nazaire Raid"); and [Special Operations Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Operations_Executive "Special Operations Executive") personnel who died in occupied Europe. The Brookwood Memorial also honours 199 Canadian servicemen and women. The memorial was placed within a military cemetery near the theatre of operations.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-64) The **Brookwood (Russia) Memorial** was erected in 1983 and dismantled in 2015. It commemorated forces of the British Commonwealth who died in Russia in [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and were buried there. The memorial was erected originally because during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") those graves were inaccessible.

## Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG/250px-Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG)

The World War I [Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial"), within the grounds of Brookwood Cemetery

Main article: [Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial")

This 4.5-acre (1.8 ha) site lies to the west of the civilian cemetery. It contains the graves of 468 American military dead from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and commemorates a further 563 with no known grave.

After the entry of the United States into the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") the American cemetery was enlarged, with burials of US servicemen beginning in April 1942. With large numbers of American personnel based in the west of England, a dedicated rail service for the transport of bodies operated from [Devonport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonport,_Devon "Devonport, Devon") to Brookwood. By August 1944, over 3,600 bodies had been buried in the American Military Cemetery. At this time burials were discontinued, and US casualties were from then on buried at [Cambridge American Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Cambridge American Cemetery and Memorial").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

On the authority of the [Quartermaster General of the United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartermaster_General_of_the_United_States_Army "Quartermaster General of the United States Army"), the US servicemen buried at Brookwood during the Second World War were exhumed in January–May 1948.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200667-66) Those whose next of kin requested it were shipped to the United States for reburial,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200667-66) and the remaining bodies were transferred to the new cemetery outside Cambridge.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

Brookwood American Cemetery had also been the burial site for those US servicemen executed while serving in the United Kingdom, whose bodies had been carried to Brookwood by rail from the American execution facilities at [Shepton Mallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepton_Mallet_(HM_Prison) "Shepton Mallet (HM Prison)").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65) Initially, the remains of the eighteen American prisoners executed at Shepton Mallet were interred in unmarked graves at "Plot X". Plot X was in a distant corner of the cemetery, away from the other plots and next to toolsheds and a compost heap. Executed prisoners interred there were not given coffins, but were put into cotton mattress covers and buried in individual graves under numbered markers. Plot X had room for one hundred graves and was the first effort to segregate executed Army prisoners from those who had been killed in combat.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPolmarAllen2012196-67) They were not transferred to Cambridge in 1948, but instead reburied in unmarked graves at [Oise-Aisne American Cemetery Plot E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Burials_at_Oise-Aisne_American_Cemetery_Plot_E "List of Burials at Oise-Aisne American Cemetery Plot E"), a dedicated site for US servicemen executed during the Second World War.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65) (One of those executed, David Cobb, was not transferred to Plot E but was repatriated to the US and reburied in [Dothan, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dothan,_Alabama "Dothan, Alabama") in 1949.) Following the removal of the US war graves, the site in which they had been buried was divided into cemeteries for the [Free French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_French "Free French") forces and Italian prisoners of war.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

It is administered by the [American Battle Monuments Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Battle_Monuments_Commission "American Battle Monuments Commission"). Close by are military cemeteries and monuments of the British Commonwealth and other allied nations.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-69)

## Parsee (Zoroastrian) burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Parsee (Zoroastrian) burial ground")]

Brookwood Cemetery contains the only [Parsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsee "Parsee")/[Zoroastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrian "Zoroastrian") burial ground in Europe. Opened in November 1862 due to the first recorded death of a Parsee in Britain, it was redesigned in 1901 by Sir [George Birdwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Birdwood "George Birdwood") to the traditional plan of the Persian paradise. As Clarke [[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-70) describes, "The Wadia mausoleum, in the centre of the ground, represents the seven-staged 'heavenly mountain' from which the four paths lead east, south, west and north. The new aviary, or Fire Temple, is based on designs from the ruins of a double gateway of the Palace of Xerxes, and replaced the original agiary. The planting was a herbaceous plants and flowering shrubs and trees that were originally native to Persia." Some notable burials include that of [Jamshedji Tata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamshedji_Tata "Jamshedji Tata") (3 March 1839 – 19 May 1904) an Indian industrialist and philanthropist who founded the [Tata Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_Group "Tata Group"), India's biggest conglomerate company. He established the city of Jamshedpur, D.H. Hakim, one of the founding members of the London Zoroastrian Association and whose death in 1862 was the catalyst for the opening of the burial grounds, and Bapsybanoo, Dowager Marchioness of Winchester (1902-1995), the flamboyant daughter of the Most Reverend Khurshedji Pavry, high priest of the Parsees in India.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-71)

## Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Location")]

Brookwood Cemetery is served by [Brookwood railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_railway_station "Brookwood railway station"), and is located on both sides of Cemetery Pales in Woking. The Cemetery office is located in Glades House.

**Brookwood Cemetery**, also known as the **London Necropolis**, is a burial ground in [Brookwood, Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood,_Surrey "Brookwood, Surrey"), England. It is the largest cemetery in the United Kingdom and one of the largest in Europe. The cemetery is listed a Grade I site in the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-NHLE-9)

The [Church of St Edward the Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St_Edward_the_Martyr,_Brookwood "Church of St Edward the Martyr, Brookwood") with its community of [Greek Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Orthodox_Church "Greek Orthodox Church") monks is located in the cemetery grounds.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

Brookwood Cemetery was conceived by the [London Necropolis Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_Company "London Necropolis Company") (LNC) in 1849 to house [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")'s deceased, at a time when the capital was finding it difficult to accommodate its increasing population, both living and dead. The cemetery is said to have been landscaped by [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect")[William Tite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tite "William Tite"), but this is disputed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-10)

Brookwood Cemetery's initial owner was incorporated by Act of Parliament in 1852, and the cemetery was consecrated by [Charles Sumner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sumner_(bishop) "Charles Sumner (bishop)"), [Bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"), on 7 November 1854 (apart from its northern section, reserved for Nonconformists). It was opened to the public on 13 November 1854 when the first burials took place. It was the largest [cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") in the world in 1854, but has since lost that distinction.

In 1857 actor [John W. Anson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_W._Anson "John W. Anson") acquired 1 acre (4,000 m 2) of land there, the Actors' Acre, for the 'Dramatic, Equestrian and Musical Sick Fund Association' as a burial place for actors and their relatives.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-11)

In 1858 the London Necropolis Company sold 64 acres (26 ha) of the extra land to the government for the building of [Woking Convict Invalid Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Convict_Invalid_Prison "Woking Convict Invalid Prison").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-12)

### Necropolis Railway

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Necropolis Railway")]

Main article: [London Necropolis Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_Railway "London Necropolis Railway")

Brookwood originally was accessible by rail from a special station – the [London Necropolis railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Necropolis_railway_station "London Necropolis railway station") – next to [Waterloo station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Waterloo_station "London Waterloo station") in Central London. Trains had passenger carriages reserved for different classes and other carriages for coffins (also for different classes), and ran into the cemetery on a dedicated branch from the adjoining [South West Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Main_Line "South West Main Line") – there was a junction just to the west of [Brookwood station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_railway_station "Brookwood railway station"). From there, passengers and coffins were transported by [horse-drawn vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse-drawn_vehicles "Horse-drawn vehicles"). The original London Necropolis station was relocated in 1902 but its successor was demolished after suffering bomb damage during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

[![Image 7: Railway ticket labelled "Southern Railways London Necropolis Coffin Ticket, Waterloo to Brookwood, Third Class](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/d/dd/Brookwood_Coffin_Ticket.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_Coffin_Ticket.jpg)

Third class coffin ticket, issued between April–September 1925.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006162-13)

Return tickets were issued for mourners and single tickets for the dead.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006150-14)

There were two stations in the cemetery: _North_ for non-conformists and _South_ for Anglicans. Their platforms still exist along the path called Railway Avenue. For visitors wishing to use the South West Main Line, Brookwood station has provided direct access since June 1864. A very short piece of commemorative track, with signpost and plaque, purposefully gives way to a grass field and recollects the old final stage of the journey of the deceased.

It was the cholera epidemic of 1848 that led two industrialists to develop this high burial site. It was at first a controversial project. The Bishop of London condemned the "offensive" despatch of first-, second- and third-class corpses in the same carriages, so this had to be modified.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Early burials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early burials")]

The LNC offered three classes of funerals:

*   A first class funeral allowed buyers to select the grave site of their choice anywhere in the cemetery. The LNC charged extra for burials in some designated special sites.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15) At the time of opening prices began at £2 10[s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling_(British_coin) "Shilling (British coin)") (about £240 in 2025 terms) for a basic 9-by-4-foot (2.7 m ×1.2 m) with no special coffin specifications.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-inflation-UK-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15) It was expected by the LNC that those using first class graves would erect a permanent memorial of some kind in due course following the funeral.
*   Second class funerals cost £1 (about £96 in 2025 terms) and allowed some control over the burial location.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200681-17) The right to erect a permanent memorial cost an additional 10 [shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling_(British_coin) "Shilling (British coin)") (about £48 in 2025 terms); if a permanent memorial was not erected the LNC reserved the right to re-use the grave in future.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-inflation-UK-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200683-15)
*   Third class funerals were reserved for pauper funerals; those buried at [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish") expense in the section of the cemetery designated for that parish. Although the LNC was forbidden from using mass graves (other than the burial of next of kin in the same grave) and thus even the lowest class of funeral provided a separate grave for the deceased, third class funerals were not granted the right to erect a permanent memorial on the site.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200681-17) (The families of those buried could pay afterwards to upgrade a third class grave to a higher class if they later wanted to erect a memorial, but this practice was rare.)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200416-18) Despite this, Brookwood's pauper graves granted more dignity to the deceased than did other graveyards and cemeteries of the period, all of which other than Brookwood continued the practice of mass graves for the poor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006103-19)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg/250px-Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henry_Goldfinch_Grave_Brookwood_2016.jpg)

The monument to [Sir Henry Goldfinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Goldfinch "Henry Goldfinch") is the earliest in the cemetery. Brookwood Columbarian in background left.

Brookwood was one of the few cemeteries to permit burials on Sundays, which made it a popular choice with the poor as it allowed people to attend funerals without the need to take a day off work.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200691-20) As theatrical performances were banned on Sundays at this time, it also made Brookwood a popular choice for the burial of actors for the same reason, to the extent that actors were provided with a dedicated section of the cemetery near the station entrance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006103-19)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200693-21)

While the majority of burials conducted by the LNC (around 80%) were pauper funerals on behalf of London parishes and prisons,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200416-18) the LNC also reached agreement with a number of societies, guilds, religious bodies and similar organisations (such as [Woking Convict Invalid Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Convict_Invalid_Prison "Woking Convict Invalid Prison") and [Tothill Fields House of Correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tothill_Fields_Bridewell "Tothill Fields Bridewell")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-22)). The LNC provided dedicated sections of the cemetery for these groups, on the basis that those who had lived or worked together in life could remain together after death.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200415%E2%80%9316-23) Although the LNC was never able to gain the domination of London's funeral industry for which its founders had hoped, it was very successful at targeting specialist groups of artisans and trades, to the extent that it became nicknamed "the Westminster Abbey of the middle classes".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200420-24) The [Royal Hospital Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Hospital_Chelsea "Royal Hospital Chelsea"), which previously buried their inmate pensioners at [Brompton Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brompton_Cemetery "Brompton Cemetery") in Chelsea, have used Brookwood Cemetery, where they have two plots, since 1893.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-Philpot2018-25)

A large number of these dedicated plots were established, ranging from [Chelsea Pensioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Pensioners "Chelsea Pensioners") and the [Ancient Order of Foresters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Order_of_Foresters "Ancient Order of Foresters") to the [Corps of Commissionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corps_of_Commissionaires "Corps of Commissionaires") and the LSWR.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200415-26) The Nonconformist cemetery also includes a [Parsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsee "Parsee") burial ground established in 1862, which as of 2011[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit) remained the only [Zoroastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrianism "Zoroastrianism") burial ground in Europe.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2004233-27) Dedicated sections in the Anglican cemetery were also reserved for burials from those parishes which had made burial arrangements with the LNC.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28)

The first burial was of the [stillborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stillbirth "Stillbirth") twins of a Mr and Mrs Hore of Ewer Street, [The Borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Borough,_London "The Borough, London").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) The Hore twins, along with the other burials on the first day, were pauper funerals and buried in unmarked graves.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) The first burial at Brookwood with a permanent memorial was that of Lieutenant-General [Sir Henry Goldfinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Goldfinch "Henry Goldfinch"), buried on 25 November 1854, the 26th person to be buried in the cemetery.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413%E2%80%9314-30) The first permanent memorial erected in the Nonconformist section of the cemetery was that of Charles Milligan Hogg, son of botanist [Robert Hogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hogg_(biologist) "Robert Hogg (biologist)"), buried on 12 December 1854.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200414-31) Goldfinch and Hogg's graves are not the oldest monuments in the cemetery, as on occasion gravestones were relocated and re-erected during the relocation of existing burial grounds to Brookwood.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006112-32)

[![Image 9: Grassy area lined with giant sequoia trees, with occasional scattered gravestones](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg/250px-Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_cemetery_5.jpg)

The rate of burials was much lower than anticipated by the London Necropolis Company and around 80% of graves are unmarked, making Brookwood distinctively uncluttered when compared to other cemeteries.

Over 235,000 people have been buried there.

### Reburials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reburials")]

The massive London civil engineering projects of the mid-19th century—the railways, the [sewer system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_sewerage_system "London sewerage system") and from the 1860s the precursors to the [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground")—often necessitated the demolition of existing churchyards.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006111-33) The first major relocation took place in 1862, when the construction of [Charing Cross railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross_railway_station "Charing Cross railway station") and the routes into it necessitated the demolition of the burial ground of Cure's College in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), which uncovered at least 7,950 bodies.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006111-33) These were packed into 220 large containers, each containing 26 adults plus children, and shipped on the London Necropolis Railway to Brookwood for reburial, along with at least some of the existing headstones from the cemetery.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006112-32)

At least 21 London burial grounds were relocated to Brookwood via the railway, along with numerous others relocated by road following the railway's closure. Churches whose graves were relocated included:

*   [St Michael, Crooked Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael,_Crooked_Lane "St Michael, Crooked Lane") (demolished 1831, burial ground cleared 1987)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-34)
*   [St Antholin, Budge Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Antholin,_Budge_Row "St Antholin, Budge Row") (demolished 1875)
*   [All-Hallows-the-Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Hallows-the-Great "All-Hallows-the-Great") (demolished 1894)
*   [St Magnus-the-Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Magnus-the-Martyr "St Magnus-the-Martyr") (remains removed from crypt 1894)
*   [All-Hallows-the-Less](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Hallows-the-Less "All-Hallows-the-Less") (destroyed in the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London"), remains removed 1896)
*   [St Michael Wood Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael_Wood_Street "St Michael Wood Street") (demolished 1897)
*   [St Mildred, Bread Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mildred,_Bread_Street "St Mildred, Bread Street") (remains removed 1898, church destroyed in [London Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Blitz "London Blitz") 1941)
*   [St George the Martyr, Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George_the_Martyr,_Southwark "St George the Martyr, Southwark") (remains removed 1899)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-35)
*   [St George Botolph Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George_Botolph_Lane "St George Botolph Lane") (demolished 1904)
*   [St Peter's Church, Eaton Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Peter's_Church,_Eaton_Square "St Peter's Church, Eaton Square") (crypt cleared 1951)
*   [St Marylebone Parish Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Marylebone_Parish_Church "St Marylebone Parish Church") (remains from crypt removed 1987)
*   [St Luke Old Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Luke_Old_Street "St Luke Old Street") (closed 1959, remains from crypt removed 2000)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-36)
*   [St James's Church, Piccadilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly "St James's Church, Piccadilly") (remains removed from St. James's Garden, established 1878 on the former burial grounds of the church, from 2017–2020 due to [HS2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HS2 "HS2") terminal construction at [Euston Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euston_Station "Euston Station")) - the largest exhumation in British history.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-37)
*   The unconsecrated [Cross Bones Graveyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Bones_Graveyard "Cross Bones Graveyard") in Southwark (closed 1853, many remains removed in successive years)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-38)

### Brookwood Cemetery and cremation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Brookwood Cemetery and cremation")]

In 1878, the LNC sold an isolated piece of its land at Brookwood, close to [St John's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's,_Woking "St John's, Woking") village, to the [Cremation Society of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremation_Society_of_Great_Britain "Cremation Society of Great Britain"), on which they built [Woking Crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_Crematorium "Woking Crematorium"), the first in Britain, in 1879.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200418-39) While the LNC never built its own crematorium, in 1910, [Lord Cadogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cadogan,_5th_Earl_Cadogan "George Cadogan, 5th Earl Cadogan") decided he no longer wanted to be interred in the mausoleum he had commissioned at Brookwood. This building, the largest mausoleum in the cemetery, was bought by the LNC, fitted with shelves and niches to hold urns, and used as a dedicated [columbarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbarium "Columbarium") from then on.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200424-40)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg/250px-Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Columbarium_Brookwood_Cemetery_2016.jpg)

Brookwood Columbarium, built as a mausoleum for Lord Cadogan but converted in 1910 for the storage of cremation urns

After 1945 cremation, up to that time an uncommon practice, became increasingly popular in Britain.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2004250-41) In 1946, the LNC obtained consent to build their own crematorium on a section of the Nonconformist cemetery which had been set aside for pauper burials, but chose not to proceed.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42) Instead, in 1945, the LNC began the construction of the Glades of Remembrance, a wooded area dedicated to the burial of cremated remains.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42) These were dedicated by [Henry Montgomery Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Montgomery_Campbell "Henry Montgomery Campbell"), [Bishop of Guildford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Guildford "Bishop of Guildford") in 1950.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200428-42)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-43) Intentionally designed for informality, traditional gravestones and memorials were prohibited, and burials were marked only by small 2-to-3-inch (5.1 to 7.6 cm) stones.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200429-44)
