In the next decade, the cemetery came closest to having its own crematorium. Following the closure of the two Brookwood railway stations, the land surrounding the site of South station and the station's two Anglican chapels was redundant. As part of the  ([4 & 5 Eliz. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_&_5_Eliz._2 "4 & 5 Eliz. 2"). c. lxviii), the LNC obtained parliamentary consent to convert the disused original Anglican chapel into a crematorium, using the newer chapel for funeral services and the station building for coffin storage and as a refreshment room for those attending cremations.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200430-45) Suffering cash flow problems and distracted by a succession of hostile takeover bids, the LNC management never proceeded with the scheme and the buildings fell into disuse.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200430-45) The station building was demolished after being damaged by a fire in 1972, although the platform remained intact.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200669-46)

### Horticultural

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Horticultural")]

With the ambition for it to become London's sole burial site in perpetuity, the LNC were aware that if their plans were successful, their Necropolis would become a site of major national importance.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29) As a consequence, the cemetery was designed with attractiveness in mind, in contrast to the squalid and congested London burial grounds and the newer suburban cemeteries which were already becoming crowded.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-Times-47)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200413-29)

The LNC aimed to create an atmosphere of perpetual spring in the cemetery, and chose the plants for the cemetery accordingly. It had already been noted that [evergreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen "Evergreen") plants from North America thrived in the local soil.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28) Robert Donald, the owner of an [arboretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboretum "Arboretum") near Woking, was contracted to supply the trees and shrubs for the cemetery.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200410%E2%80%9311-48) The railway line through the cemetery and the major roads and paths within the cemetery were lined with [giant sequoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoiadendron_giganteum "Sequoiadendron giganteum") trees, the first significant planting of these trees (only introduced to Europe in 1853) in Britain.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28) As well as the giant sequoias (also known as _Wellingtonia_ after the recently deceased [Duke of Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington "Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington")), the grounds were heavily planted with [magnolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnolia "Magnolia"), [rhododendron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhododendron "Rhododendron"), [coastal redwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_sempervirens "Sequoia sempervirens"), [azalea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azalea "Azalea"), [andromeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieris_(plant) "Pieris (plant)") and [monkeypuzzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araucaria_araucana "Araucaria araucana"), with the intention of creating perpetual greenery with large numbers of flowers and a strong floral scent throughout the cemetery.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200411-28)

In later years the original planting of the cemetery was supplemented by numerous other tree species planted by the LNC, as well as many plants planted by mourners at burial sites and around mausolea. Between the end of LNC independence in 1959 and the cemetery's purchase by [Ramadan Güney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramadan_G%C3%BCney "Ramadan Güney") in 1985 cemetery maintenance was drastically reduced, and the spread of various plant types caused many of the non-military sections of the cemetery to revert to wilderness in this period.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200431-49)

### 20th and 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 20th and 21st centuries")]

In August 1914, on the outbreak of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), the LNC offered to donate to the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office")1 acre (4,000 m 2) of land "for the free interment of soldiers and sailors who have returned from the front wounded and may subsequently die". The offer was not taken up until 1917, when a section of the cemetery was set aside as Brookwood Military Cemetery, used for the burials of service personnel who died in the [London District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_District_(British_Army) "London District (British Army)").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200424-40) This purpose built cemetery came to accommodate further dead from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

In the meantime, 141 Commonwealth service personnel were buried from London in scattered graves throughout the cemetery, apart from a small Nurses' Plot in St Peter's Avenue in the Westminster field (where are buried nurses from [Millbank Military Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Alexandra_Military_Hospital "Queen Alexandra Military Hospital")) and an Indian plot (including one unidentified soldier) in the North-West corner.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgcbc-50)

In World War II 51 Commonwealth service personnel were buried in the civilian cemetery, where there are also buried five foreign national servicemen whose graves the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") (CWGC) additionally care for.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgcbc-50) A military memorial to the missing from that war was built in 1958 by the CWGC.

[Edward the Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Martyr "Edward the Martyr"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-51) King of England, was memorialised here. His relics are kept nearby in [St Edward the Martyr Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Edward_the_Martyr_Orthodox_Church "St Edward the Martyr Orthodox Church").

The London Necropolis Company was taken over by Alliance Property in 1959[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200631-52) and the company was gradually divested of land and investments until by 1973, the cemetery was an independent entity. The cemetery changed hands between various development companies in the 1970s, during which time the cemetery maintenance was neglected: 1970 Cornwall Property (Holdings) Ltd, 1971 Great Southern Group, 1973 Maximillian Investments.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200631%E2%80%9332-53) Maximillian Investments secured the passing of the **Brookwood Cemetery Act 1975** (c. xxxv) which authorised them to sell unused parts of the cemetery[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200632-54) and a few areas were sold for development.

In 1985, Ramadan Güney acquired Brookwood Cemetery from the owner Mr D. J. T. Dally, who was previously the cemetery manager.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200635-7) The purchase evolved from Güney's role as Chairman of the UK Turkish Islamic Trust, which wanted suitable burial facilities for its members.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-BrookwoodCemetery-6) The Brookwood Cemetery Society was founded in 1992 to organise events, promote the site's history and support restoration work. After Güney's death in 2006 he was buried in the cemetery and ownership passed to his children (by his late wife) and operated by his son Erkin, a director at the cemetery for almost 30 years. Diane Holliday, Güney's partner of 6 years, was "frozen out" from the operating company and then dismissed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DecisionUpheld-4) In 2011, the inheritance of the cemetery was successfully challenged by Diane Holliday and her adult son Kevin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DisputeResolved-5) This decision was upheld by the High Court on appeal in 2012.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-DecisionUpheld-4) In 2014, Diane Holliday sold the cemetery to [Woking Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking_(borough) "Woking (borough)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-council-3)

In 2017, work began on the exhumation of the remains of approximately 40,000 to 50,000 people who were interred at the [former burial ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly#Detached_burial_ground "St James's Church, Piccadilly") of [St. James's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Piccadilly "St James's Church, Piccadilly")[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-55) due to construction of the new [HS2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HS2 "HS2") terminal at [Euston Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euston_Station "Euston Station") in London.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-stjameshs2-56) The former burial ground had been in use between 1790 and 1853 before the cemetery became St James's Gardens in 1878. The grounds had been utilised as public park space until they were closed in 2017 at the outset of construction.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-stjameshs2-56) A large part of the exhumation project consisted of a multi-year cataloguing and study of the remains by [osteo-archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoarchaeology "Osteoarchaeology"), part of which was documented by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-57) In 2020 it was announced that it had been agreed by the Woking Council and HS2 that the remains were to be re-interred in a new grassland plot on the south side of Brookwood Cemetery.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-58) The exhumations and study began in October 2018 and the re-interment at Brookwood took place sometime around August 2020 to November 2020.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-clarke-59) At around 50,000 individual remains, it is thought to be the largest single reburial project in the history of Brookwood.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-clarke-59)

## Brookwood Military Cemetery and memorials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Brookwood Military Cemetery and memorials")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG/330px-The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Brookwood_Memorial.JPG)

The Brookwood Memorial, built in 1958 and designed by [Ralph Hobday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Hobday "Ralph Hobday")

**Brookwood Military Cemetery** covers about 37 acres (15 ha) and is the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the United Kingdom. The land was set aside during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") to provide a burial site for men and women of Commonwealth and American armed forces who died in the United Kingdom of wounds and other causes. It now contains 1,601 Commonwealth burials from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 3,476 from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (the latter including 3 unidentified [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") and 2 unidentified [Canadian airmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Air_Force "Royal Canadian Air Force")).

Within this, there is a particularly large Canadian section, which includes 43 men who died of wounds following the [Dieppe Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieppe_Raid "Dieppe Raid") in August 1942. Two dozen Muslim dead were also later transferred here in 1968 from the [Muslim Burial Ground at Horsell Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Burial_Ground,_Horsell_Common "Muslim Burial Ground, Horsell Common"). There is a large [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") section in the southeast corner of the cemetery which includes graves of Czech and United States nationals who died serving in the RAF.

The cemetery also has 786 non-Commonwealth war graves, including 28 unidentified French, besides eight German dead from World War I and 46 from World War II.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-60) It also contains Polish (84 graves), Czech, Belgian (46 graves), Dutch (seven graves) and Italian (over 300 graves) sections.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-61) Except for [Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day "Christmas Day") and [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day"), this cemetery is open to the public from 8am to sunset Monday to Friday, and 9am to sunset Saturdays and Sundays.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-62)

The **Brookwood 1914–1918 Memorial** originally stood at the northeastern end of the 1914–1918 Plot. The new memorial that replaced it was created in 2004, and currently (23 June 2025) commemorates 391 Commonwealth service personnel who died in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") in the United Kingdom but have no known grave. The majority of the casualties commemorated on the Brookwood 1914–1918 Memorial are servicemen and women identified by the In From The Cold Project as having died while in care of their families and were not commemorated by the Commission at the time. (Those whose graves are subsequently discovered become commemorated under the respective cemetery.)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-63)

The **Brookwood 1939-1945 Memorial** stands at the southern end of the Canadian section of the cemetery and commemorates 3,428 Commonwealth men and women who died during the Second World War and have no known grave. This includes commandos killed in the [Dieppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieppe_Raid "Dieppe Raid") and [St Nazaire Raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Nazaire_Raid "St Nazaire Raid"); and [Special Operations Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Operations_Executive "Special Operations Executive") personnel who died in occupied Europe. The Brookwood Memorial also honours 199 Canadian servicemen and women. The memorial was placed within a military cemetery near the theatre of operations.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-64) The **Brookwood (Russia) Memorial** was erected in 1983 and dismantled in 2015. It commemorated forces of the British Commonwealth who died in Russia in [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and were buried there. The memorial was erected originally because during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") those graves were inaccessible.

## Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG/250px-Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brookwood_American_Military_Chapel.JPG)

The World War I [Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial"), within the grounds of Brookwood Cemetery

Main article: [Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial")

This 4.5-acre (1.8 ha) site lies to the west of the civilian cemetery. It contains the graves of 468 American military dead from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and commemorates a further 563 with no known grave.

After the entry of the United States into the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") the American cemetery was enlarged, with burials of US servicemen beginning in April 1942. With large numbers of American personnel based in the west of England, a dedicated rail service for the transport of bodies operated from [Devonport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonport,_Devon "Devonport, Devon") to Brookwood. By August 1944, over 3,600 bodies had been buried in the American Military Cemetery. At this time burials were discontinued, and US casualties were from then on buried at [Cambridge American Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_American_Cemetery_and_Memorial "Cambridge American Cemetery and Memorial").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

On the authority of the [Quartermaster General of the United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartermaster_General_of_the_United_States_Army "Quartermaster General of the United States Army"), the US servicemen buried at Brookwood during the Second World War were exhumed in January–May 1948.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200667-66) Those whose next of kin requested it were shipped to the United States for reburial,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke200667-66) and the remaining bodies were transferred to the new cemetery outside Cambridge.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

Brookwood American Cemetery had also been the burial site for those US servicemen executed while serving in the United Kingdom, whose bodies had been carried to Brookwood by rail from the American execution facilities at [Shepton Mallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepton_Mallet_(HM_Prison) "Shepton Mallet (HM Prison)").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65) Initially, the remains of the eighteen American prisoners executed at Shepton Mallet were interred in unmarked graves at "Plot X". Plot X was in a distant corner of the cemetery, away from the other plots and next to toolsheds and a compost heap. Executed prisoners interred there were not given coffins, but were put into cotton mattress covers and buried in individual graves under numbered markers. Plot X had room for one hundred graves and was the first effort to segregate executed Army prisoners from those who had been killed in combat.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPolmarAllen2012196-67) They were not transferred to Cambridge in 1948, but instead reburied in unmarked graves at [Oise-Aisne American Cemetery Plot E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Burials_at_Oise-Aisne_American_Cemetery_Plot_E "List of Burials at Oise-Aisne American Cemetery Plot E"), a dedicated site for US servicemen executed during the Second World War.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65) (One of those executed, David Cobb, was not transferred to Plot E but was repatriated to the US and reburied in [Dothan, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dothan,_Alabama "Dothan, Alabama") in 1949.) Following the removal of the US war graves, the site in which they had been buried was divided into cemeteries for the [Free French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_French "Free French") forces and Italian prisoners of war.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2006126-65)

It is administered by the [American Battle Monuments Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Battle_Monuments_Commission "American Battle Monuments Commission"). Close by are military cemeteries and monuments of the British Commonwealth and other allied nations.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-69)

## Parsee (Zoroastrian) burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Parsee (Zoroastrian) burial ground")]

Brookwood Cemetery contains the only [Parsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsee "Parsee")/[Zoroastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrian "Zoroastrian") burial ground in Europe. Opened in November 1862 due to the first recorded death of a Parsee in Britain, it was redesigned in 1901 by Sir [George Birdwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Birdwood "George Birdwood") to the traditional plan of the Persian paradise. As Clarke [[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-70) describes, "The Wadia mausoleum, in the centre of the ground, represents the seven-staged 'heavenly mountain' from which the four paths lead east, south, west and north. The new aviary, or Fire Temple, is based on designs from the ruins of a double gateway of the Palace of Xerxes, and replaced the original agiary. The planting was a herbaceous plants and flowering shrubs and trees that were originally native to Persia." Some notable burials include that of [Jamshedji Tata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamshedji_Tata "Jamshedji Tata") (3 March 1839 – 19 May 1904) an Indian industrialist and philanthropist who founded the [Tata Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_Group "Tata Group"), India's biggest conglomerate company. He established the city of Jamshedpur, D.H. Hakim, one of the founding members of the London Zoroastrian Association and whose death in 1862 was the catalyst for the opening of the burial grounds, and Bapsybanoo, Dowager Marchioness of Winchester (1902-1995), the flamboyant daughter of the Most Reverend Khurshedji Pavry, high priest of the Parsees in India.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery#cite_note-71)

## Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brookwood_Cemetery&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Location")]

Brookwood Cemetery is served by [Brookwood railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_railway_station "Brookwood railway station"), and is located on both sides of Cemetery Pales in Woking. The Cemetery office is located in Glades House.

'''East Finchley Cemetery''' is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [[East Finchley]]. Although it is in the [[London Borough of Barnet]], it is owned and managed by the [[City of Westminster]].<ref name=cemetery>[http://www.westminster.gov.uk/communityandliving/burials/eastfinchley.cfm ''East Finchley Cemetery''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081026092317/http://www.westminster.gov.uk/communityandliving/burials/eastfinchley.cfm |date=2008-10-26 }} (City of Westminster) accessed 26 January 2006</ref>

==History and characteristics==
The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased {{convert|47|acre|km2|2}} of Newmarket Farm in 1854;<ref name=cemetery/> and the cemetery, then known as '''St Marylebone Cemetery''', was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [[Lebanon Cedar]] trees planted on the front lawn. The [[crematorium]] was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [[Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone]] – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.<ref name=cemetery/>

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [[Westminster cemeteries scandal]]. The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. <ref>{{cite news|title=Westminster back in the dock|first=David|last=Hencke|date=10 December 1998|work=[[The Guardian]]|location=London|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/1998/dec/10/uk.politicalnews|access-date=26 November 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Council to buy back land it sold off for 5p |first=David |last=Millward |date=20 April 2006 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|location=London |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1516167/Council-to-buy-back-land-it-sold-off-for-5p.html |access-date=6 October 2011}}</ref> This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [[National Heritage List for England]].

The [[Anglican]] chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [[listed building|listed chapel]],<ref>{{NHLE |num=1064767 |access-date=26 January 2006}}</ref> as is the crematorium.<ref name=NHLECrem>{{NHLE|num=1359115|desc=Crematorium and Chapel, St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>
The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.<ref>[https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1064768 Entry on the Historic England website]</ref>

The monuments to [[Thomas Skarratt Hall]] (supposedly based on the [[Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus]], it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1249532|desc=Monument to Thomas Skarratt Hall, West Avenue, Plot H7|access-date=29 September 2018}}</ref> Harry Ripley (by [[William Reid Dick]]),<ref name=NHLERipley>{{NHLE|num=1359116|desc=Monument to Harry Ripley|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> [[Peter Nicol Russell]],<ref name="NHLERussell">{{NHLE|num=1188637|desc=Monument to Sir Peter Nicol Russell Engineer in St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> Thomas Tate (by [[Frank Lynn Jenkins]]),<ref name=NHLETate>{{NHLE|num=1064758|desc=Monument to Sir Thomas Tate, St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> and the mausoleum (by [[Arthur Blomfield]]) of [[Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk]] and his wife and son, are all [[Grade II listed]].<ref name=NHLEGlenesk>{{NHLE|num=1064757|desc=Glenesk Mausoleum|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>

The cemetery was awarded a [[Green Flag Award]] in 2007, 2008 and 2009.<ref name=cemetery/> It is also a [[Site of Nature Conservation Interest|Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation]].<ref name=GIGL>{{cite web|url=http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/siteDetails.aspx?sID=BaL08&sType=sinc|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224022212/http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/siteDetails.aspx?sID=BaL08&sType=sinc|url-status=dead|archive-date=24 December 2012|title=East Finchley Cemetery|publisher=Greenspace Information for Greater London|year=2006|access-date=9 September 2012}}</ref><ref name=map>{{cite web|url=http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/map.aspx |title=iGiGL – helping you find London's parks and wildlife sites |publisher=Greenspace Information for Greater London |year=2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121129124243/http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/map.aspx |archive-date=29 November 2012 }}</ref>

'''East Finchley Cemetery''' is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [[East Finchley]]. Although it is in the [[London Borough of Barnet]], it is owned and managed by the [[City of Westminster]].<ref name=cemetery>[http://www.westminster.gov.uk/communityandliving/burials/eastfinchley.cfm ''East Finchley Cemetery''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081026092317/http://www.westminster.gov.uk/communityandliving/burials/eastfinchley.cfm |date=2008-10-26 }} (City of Westminster) accessed 26 January 2006</ref>

==History and characteristics==
The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased {{convert|47|acre|km2|2}} of Newmarket Farm in 1854;<ref name=cemetery/> and the cemetery, then known as '''St Marylebone Cemetery''', was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [[Lebanon Cedar]] trees planted on the front lawn. The [[crematorium]] was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [[Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone]] – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.<ref name=cemetery/>

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [[Westminster cemeteries scandal]]. The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. <ref>{{cite news|title=Westminster back in the dock|first=David|last=Hencke|date=10 December 1998|work=[[The Guardian]]|location=London|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/1998/dec/10/uk.politicalnews|access-date=26 November 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Council to buy back land it sold off for 5p |first=David |last=Millward |date=20 April 2006 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|location=London |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1516167/Council-to-buy-back-land-it-sold-off-for-5p.html |access-date=6 October 2011}}</ref> This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [[National Heritage List for England]].

The [[Anglican]] chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [[listed building|listed chapel]],<ref>{{NHLE |num=1064767 |access-date=26 January 2006}}</ref> as is the crematorium.<ref name=NHLECrem>{{NHLE|num=1359115|desc=Crematorium and Chapel, St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>
The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.<ref>[https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1064768 Entry on the Historic England website]</ref>

The monuments to [[Thomas Skarratt Hall]] (supposedly based on the [[Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus]], it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1249532|desc=Monument to Thomas Skarratt Hall, West Avenue, Plot H7|access-date=29 September 2018}}</ref> Harry Ripley (by [[William Reid Dick]]),<ref name=NHLERipley>{{NHLE|num=1359116|desc=Monument to Harry Ripley|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> [[Peter Nicol Russell]],<ref name="NHLERussell">{{NHLE|num=1188637|desc=Monument to Sir Peter Nicol Russell Engineer in St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> Thomas Tate (by [[Frank Lynn Jenkins]]),<ref name=NHLETate>{{NHLE|num=1064758|desc=Monument to Sir Thomas Tate, St Marylebone Cemetery|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref> and the mausoleum (by [[Arthur Blomfield]]) of [[Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk]] and his wife and son, are all [[Grade II listed]].<ref name=NHLEGlenesk>{{NHLE|num=1064757|desc=Glenesk Mausoleum|access-date=4 October 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>

The cemetery was awarded a [[Green Flag Award]] in 2007, 2008 and 2009.<ref name=cemetery/> It is also a [[Site of Nature Conservation Interest|Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation]].<ref name=GIGL>{{cite web|url=http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/siteDetails.aspx?sID=BaL08&sType=sinc|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224022212/http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/siteDetails.aspx?sID=BaL08&sType=sinc|url-status=dead|archive-date=24 December 2012|title=East Finchley Cemetery|publisher=Greenspace Information for Greater London|year=2006|access-date=9 September 2012}}</ref><ref name=map>{{cite web|url=http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/map.aspx |title=iGiGL – helping you find London's parks and wildlife sites |publisher=Greenspace Information for Greater London |year=2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121129124243/http://www.gigl.org.uk/igigl/map.aspx |archive-date=29 November 2012 }}</ref>

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and characteristics")]

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War graves")]

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_Cemetery?oldid=whatever#cite_note-17)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transport")]

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**City of Westminster (Hanwell) Cemetery** is a cemetery located in [Hanwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanwell "Hanwell"), [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), [West London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_London "West London"). It is owned and managed by the City of Westminster's Parks Service.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

By the 1840s, the existing churchyards and cemeteries of London were full and almost overflowing. The Bayswater Road Cemetery and [St Mark's, North Audley Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mark's,_North_Audley_Street "St Mark's, North Audley Street") were under the control of the St. George's Hanover Square Burial Board, who were unable to find a solution until the [Metropolitan Interments Act 1850](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Interments_Act_1850 "Metropolitan Interments Act 1850") became law.

In 1853, the board purchased 12 acres (4.9 ha) in Hanwell for their exclusive use. Robert Jerrard was appointed as [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"), who designed the church and administration buildings in a [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_architecture "Victorian architecture")[Gothic revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_revival_architecture "Gothic revival architecture") style. [Consecrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consecration "Consecration") on 6 July 1854, by the [Bishop of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_London "Bishop of London")[Charles Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_James_Blomfield "Charles James Blomfield"), the total cost of cemetery and buildings was £14,741 17s 11d. The first interment took place on 2 August 1854.

In 1883, and additional 11 acres (4.5 ha) were purchased, making a total size of today of 23 acres (9.3 ha). In 1889, the cemetery was transferred to the Metropolitan Borough of the City of Westminster. The cemetery suffered extensive damage during [World War Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_Two "World War Two"), and at the end of the war in Europe a gift was given to the cemetery in the form of the renewal of the chapel's south side stained glass window, depicting a miscellany of some 30 biblical emblems.

In 1965, the cemetery came under new management in light of local government reorganisation. In 1987, the cemetery was one of three that [Shirley Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Porter "Shirley Porter")'s [Westminster City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_City_Council "Westminster City Council") controversially sold to land developers for 15p.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Cemetery#cite_note-1) However, like East Finchley and Mill Hill, it was reacquired by the new City of Westminster in 1990, and renamed at that point as their **Hanwell Cemetery.** The council undertook extensive restoration of the central buildings in 1994, and in 2001 replaced the entire roof and cleaned the exterior walls, as well as making all provisions required under the [Disability Discrimination Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_Discrimination_Act "Disability Discrimination Act").

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: War graves")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed%2C_Hanwell.JPG/250px-Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed%2C_Hanwell.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed,_Hanwell.JPG)

The memorial to the City of Westminster civilians killed during the Second World War.

There are 84 graves administered by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") – 55 from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 29 from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") – located throughout the cemetery.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgc-2) There is also a [Royal British Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_British_Legion "Royal British Legion") memorial cross in the centre of the cemetery.

A number of people killed during World War II in air raids were buried temporarily during the conflict, and then reburied afterwards. 200 residents of the City of Westminster are remembered on the civilian memorial, located near the centre of the grounds. Unveiled in 1950, it houses the grave of popular singer [Al Bowlly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Bowlly "Al Bowlly"), who was killed at his flat in [Jermyn Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jermyn_Street "Jermyn Street") during an air raid on 17 April 1941.

## Transport links

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Transport links")]

The cemetery is well connected to London's transport network, with buses [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_E3 "London Buses route E3"), [E8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_E8 "London Buses route E8"), [83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_83 "London Buses route 83") and [207](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_207 "London Buses route 207") stopping outside. The nearest [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground") stations are [Ealing Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Broadway_railway_station "Ealing Broadway railway station"), [Acton Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acton_Town_tube_station "Acton Town tube station") and [Boston Manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Manor_tube_station "Boston Manor tube station"). [Elizabeth line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_line "Elizabeth line") services stop at [Hanwell station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanwell_railway_station "Hanwell railway station"), offering services to [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") and [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_railway_station "Reading railway station"), and to [Abbey Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Wood_railway_station "Abbey Wood railway station") and [Shenfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenfield_railway_station "Shenfield railway station") via [London Paddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddington_railway_station "Paddington railway station").

**City of Westminster (Hanwell) Cemetery** is a cemetery located in [Hanwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanwell "Hanwell"), [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), [West London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_London "West London"). It is owned and managed by the City of Westminster's Parks Service.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

By the 1840s, the existing churchyards and cemeteries of London were full and almost overflowing. The Bayswater Road Cemetery and [St Mark's, North Audley Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mark's,_North_Audley_Street "St Mark's, North Audley Street") were under the control of the St. George's Hanover Square Burial Board, who were unable to find a solution until the [Metropolitan Interments Act 1850](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Interments_Act_1850 "Metropolitan Interments Act 1850") became law.

In 1853, the board purchased 12 acres (4.9 ha) in Hanwell for their exclusive use. Robert Jerrard was appointed as [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"), who designed the church and administration buildings in a [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_architecture "Victorian architecture")[Gothic revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_revival_architecture "Gothic revival architecture") style. [Consecrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consecration "Consecration") on 6 July 1854, by the [Bishop of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_London "Bishop of London")[Charles Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_James_Blomfield "Charles James Blomfield"), the total cost of cemetery and buildings was £14,741 17s 11d. The first interment took place on 2 August 1854.

In 1883, and additional 11 acres (4.5 ha) were purchased, making a total size of today of 23 acres (9.3 ha). In 1889, the cemetery was transferred to the Metropolitan Borough of the City of Westminster. The cemetery suffered extensive damage during [World War Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_Two "World War Two"), and at the end of the war in Europe a gift was given to the cemetery in the form of the renewal of the chapel's south side stained glass window, depicting a miscellany of some 30 biblical emblems.

In 1965, the cemetery came under new management in light of local government reorganisation. In 1987, the cemetery was one of three that [Shirley Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Porter "Shirley Porter")'s [Westminster City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_City_Council "Westminster City Council") controversially sold to land developers for 15p.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Cemetery#cite_note-1) However, like East Finchley and Mill Hill, it was reacquired by the new City of Westminster in 1990, and renamed at that point as their **Hanwell Cemetery.** The council undertook extensive restoration of the central buildings in 1994, and in 2001 replaced the entire roof and cleaned the exterior walls, as well as making all provisions required under the [Disability Discrimination Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_Discrimination_Act "Disability Discrimination Act").

## War graves

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: War graves")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed%2C_Hanwell.JPG/250px-Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed%2C_Hanwell.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Memorial_to_City_of_Westminster_killed,_Hanwell.JPG)

The memorial to the City of Westminster civilians killed during the Second World War.

There are 84 graves administered by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") – 55 from [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and 29 from [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") – located throughout the cemetery.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Cemetery#cite_note-cwgc-2) There is also a [Royal British Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_British_Legion "Royal British Legion") memorial cross in the centre of the cemetery.

A number of people killed during World War II in air raids were buried temporarily during the conflict, and then reburied afterwards. 200 residents of the City of Westminster are remembered on the civilian memorial, located near the centre of the grounds. Unveiled in 1950, it houses the grave of popular singer [Al Bowlly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Bowlly "Al Bowlly"), who was killed at his flat in [Jermyn Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jermyn_Street "Jermyn Street") during an air raid on 17 April 1941.

## Transport links

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_of_Westminster_Cemetery,_Hanwell&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Transport links")]

The cemetery is well connected to London's transport network, with buses [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_E3 "London Buses route E3"), [E8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_E8 "London Buses route E8"), [83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_83 "London Buses route 83") and [207](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses_route_207 "London Buses route 207") stopping outside. The nearest [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground") stations are [Ealing Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Broadway_railway_station "Ealing Broadway railway station"), [Acton Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acton_Town_tube_station "Acton Town tube station") and [Boston Manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Manor_tube_station "Boston Manor tube station"). [Elizabeth line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_line "Elizabeth line") services stop at [Hanwell station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanwell_railway_station "Hanwell railway station"), offering services to [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") and [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_railway_station "Reading railway station"), and to [Abbey Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Wood_railway_station "Abbey Wood railway station") and [Shenfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenfield_railway_station "Shenfield railway station") via [London Paddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddington_railway_station "Paddington railway station").

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-17)

## Transport

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.

**East Finchley Cemetery** is a cemetery and crematorium in East End Road, [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley "East Finchley"). Although it is in the [London Borough of Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Barnet "London Borough of Barnet"), it is owned and managed by the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1)

## History and characteristics

The St Marylebone Burial Board purchased 47 acres (0.19 km 2) of Newmarket Farm in 1854;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1) and the cemetery, then known as **St Marylebone Cemetery**, was laid out by architects Barnett & Birch after winning a competition.

Principal features are two [Lebanon Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon_Cedar "Lebanon Cedar") trees planted on the front lawn. The [crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crematorium "Crematorium") was opened in 1937.

Due to local government reorganisation, the cemetery was managed by the [Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_St_Marylebone "Metropolitan Borough of St Marylebone") – from 1900; and became the responsibility of the City of Westminster in 1965, when the cemetery became known by its current name. The cemetery contains about 22,000 interments, and remains open for burials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1)

The cemetery became a point of controversy in the early nineties when the then Leader of Westminster City Council and one of the councillors wanted the cemetery to be sold (to avoid the substantial upkeep). The cemetery also included a considerable amount of land being used at the time for plant propagation for horticultural use throughout the City of Westminster; it also provided housing for the Cemetery Keeper. After much argument at Council Meetings and against the advice of the Chief Officers concerned, the cemetery was sold, the transaction then became part of the [Westminster cemeteries scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_cemeteries_scandal "Westminster cemeteries scandal"). The council was forced, after the move had been declared unlawful, to repurchase the cemetery but was unable to buy back the crematorium. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-3) This was purchased by the London Cremation Company.

The cemetery contains a number of structures listed on the [National Heritage List for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Heritage_List_for_England "National Heritage List for England").

The [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") chapel was designed by Barnett and Birch and is a Grade II [listed chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-4) as is the crematorium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLECrem-5) The gates and lodge are also Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-6)

The monuments to [Thomas Skarratt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Skarratt_Hall "Thomas Skarratt Hall") (supposedly based on the [Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus_of_Lucius_Cornelius_Scipio_Barbatus "Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus"), it originally had four bronze angels, which were stolen in 1989),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-7) Harry Ripley (by [William Reid Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reid_Dick "William Reid Dick")),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLERipley-8)[Peter Nicol Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Nicol_Russell "Peter Nicol Russell"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLERussell-9) Thomas Tate (by [Frank Lynn Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lynn_Jenkins "Frank Lynn Jenkins")),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLETate-10) and the mausoleum (by [Arthur Blomfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blomfield "Arthur Blomfield")) of [Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Borthwick,_1st_Baron_Glenesk "Algernon Borthwick, 1st Baron Glenesk") and his wife and son, are all [Grade II listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_II_listed "Grade II listed").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-NHLEGlenesk-11)

The cemetery was awarded a Green Flag Award in 2007, 2008 and 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-cemetery-1) It is also a [Site of Local Importance for Nature Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Nature_Conservation_Interest "Site of Nature Conservation Interest").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-GIGL-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-map-13)

## War graves

There are 75 Commonwealth service war burials of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in the cemetery, most in the War Graves plot in the cemetery's northwest corner that was set aside for military burials in 1916, and 79 of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") (including two unidentified British soldiers), besides ten 'Non War graves' that the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission") maintains. A Screen Wall memorial, behind the [Cross of Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Sacrifice "Cross of Sacrifice"), records the names of the 20 World War II casualties who were cremated at the St Marylebone Crematorium. There are also special memorials to eight World War I servicemen whose graves could not be marked by headstones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_Finchley_Cemetery&printable=yes#cite_note-17)

## Transport

The cemetery on East End Road is situated near the North Circular Road (A406) and lies between [East Finchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Finchley_tube_station "East Finchley tube station") and [Finchley Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_Central_tube_station "Finchley Central tube station") stations, both on the [Northern Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Line "Northern Line"). Access by stairway is possible from bus stops on the North Circular Road.
